#3300. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3297. Skip the knockoffs: Real PITAKA aramid fiber cases start at $18.99 this Black Friday

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:

If you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

#3295. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3290. AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

#3287. Apple's AirPods Pro 3 Are $100 Off During Black Friday

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are not only my favorite earbuds I've ever owned, they might also be my favorite headphones of all time. The Pros sound great, come with excellent noise cancellation and transparency modes, and are packed with modern features that go beyond listening to music. I'd recommend these to any Apple user looking for the best overall audio experience at full price, but when they're $100 off, I actively encourage you to buy these now.

On the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. The earbuds sound great: I'm not an audiophile or a headphone reviewer, but to my ears, the Pros deliver excellent sound quality, with plenty of bass and great sound separation. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a new album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. I'm constantly switching between my iPhone, Mac, and Apple TV with mine, and they seamlessly move between each—at least, most of the time.

The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. This is a great mode for wearing your AirPods in loud environments, so you can still hear everything without the noise becoming overwhelming. To that point, these AirPods are actually FDA-certified hearing aids.

There are plenty of other features available here as well, especially if you have a compatible iPhone. AirPods Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate sensor, so you can track workouts without an Apple Watch; you can translate conversations in real time with Live Translate; "Conversation Awareness" lowers the volume of your audio and turns on transparency mode when you start speaking; and they run for eight hours on one charge with noise cancellation enabled.

This isn't an in-depth list of the AirPods Pro 3's set of features. But suffice it to say, these earbuds are worth their full MSRP of $249. So not only can I wholeheartedly recommend them at $149, but I'd say they're an easy buy if you've been thinking about picking up AirPods for yourself.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

Samsung’s 65-inch S90H is down to $1,397.99 from $1,897.99, saving you $500 on the company’s mid-range OLED TV for 2026. It’s a solid option for movie enthusiasts and gamers alike, thanks to its self-lit pixels that produce deep blacks and excellent contrast, particularly in darker scenes where conventional LED TVs can struggle with a grayish glow. You also get a high-refresh-rate display for smoother gaming.

If you have room for a bigger screen, Samsung’s 77-inch S85H is also worth a look, especially now that it’s down to $1,797.99 from $2,197.99, saving you $400. Although it sits below the S90H in Samsung’s 2026 OLED lineup, it still delivers the deep blacks, excellent contrast, and wide viewing angles that make OLED TVs appealing. The larger screen also makes it a good fit for family movie nights.

One of the biggest discounts in this roundup, the 2026 75-inch Hisense U7 is now $997.99, down from $1,999.99. Its mini-LED backlighting and local dimming are designed to deliver brighter highlights and better contrast, making it an appealing option for rooms with plenty of natural light. Gaming-focused features also make it worth a look if you plan to connect a current-generation console or gaming PC.

For a more affordable 75-inch option, Hisense's 2026 U6 Pro is down to $699.99 from $1,399.99, saving you $700. Like the U7, it uses mini-LED backlighting to improve contrast and bring out more detail in HDR movies and shows, although it sits a tier below the U7 in terms of overall picture performance. It also comes with Fire TV and Alexa+ built in, making it a convenient choice for households already using Amazon's smart home ecosystem.

The C6 is LG’s mid-range OLED evo model for 2026, and right now its 65-inch model is $1,399.99, down from its $2,699.99 launch price. It combines excellent pixel-level contrast with gaming features designed for fast-paced titles, making it a versatile choice for both movies and consoles. LG also supports Dolby Vision, which gives it an advantage over Samsung's OLEDs for viewers who regularly stream compatible HDR content.

Sony’s 65-inch Bravia 6, the entry-level OLED in its 2026 TV lineup, is now $1,198, down from $1,999.99, saving you $802. It delivers the deep blacks and excellent contrast you'd expect from the display technology, thanks to its self-lit pixels. Sony's picture processing also helps bring out fine details and natural-looking colors in movies and TV shows, while Dolby Vision support makes the most of compatible HDR content.

For the same $1,198, you can get a considerably larger screen with the 85-inch Sony Bravia 3 II, which is down from $1,599.99, saving you $402. This 2026 model uses a conventional LED panel, so it won't quite match the Bravia 6's deep blacks and contrast, but the extra 20 inches make it an appealing option for sports and family movie nights. It also has a native 120Hz refresh rate with VRR and ALLM for smoother console gaming, along with Dolby Vision support and Google TV with Gemini built in.

Toshiba’s 75-inch Z670R is down to $699.99 from $1,299.99, saving you $600 on a 2026 mini-LED TV. It combines full-array local dimming with QLED color technology for improved contrast and brighter highlights, while Toshiba’s REGZA Engine ZRi processor helps sharpen lower-resolution content. The native 144Hz refresh rate also makes it a good option for console and PC gaming, and you get Fire TV built in for streaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support.

Designed to compete with Samsung's The Frame, Toshiba's 65-inch G700 ArtVision is currently $899.99 at Amazon, down from $1,297.99, saving you $398. It's a 4K QLED TV, with a native 165Hz refresh rate, built-in Fire TV, and the same REGZA Engine ZRi processor found in the Z670R. But there's more to it than watching movies and shows, as its Ambient Mode can display over 3,000 curated artworks without a subscription, while the matte anti-glare screen and included white oak frame help it pass for a framed print on the wall.

TCL’s 98-inch F8D is down to $1,444.99 from $1,699.99, saving you $255 on a massive 2026 QLED Fire TV. It uses a high-brightness LED backlight, so you won't get the same level of contrast control as TCL's more expensive mini-LED QM models, but it still offers a native 144Hz refresh rate for smoother gaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support. And at nearly 100 inches, there's plenty of screen space to make movies, sports, and games feel more immersive.

TCL’s 75-inch QM64L is down to $699.99 after a $200 price cut—it’s the cheapest way into TCL’s 2026 QD-Mini LED lineup, and it pairs quantum dot color with local dimming for brighter highlights and better contrast in HDR movies and sports. That also makes it a good pick for a bright living room, where an OLED might not be the most practical choice. You also get a native 144Hz refresh rate for gaming and Fire TV built in

Roku’s 65-inch Plus Series is the most affordable TV in this roundup at $449.99, down from $649.99, saving you $200. This 2025 model combines a QLED panel with mini-LED backlighting and Dolby Vision support for improved contrast and richer colors when watching HDR content. It also runs the same Roku OS found on the company’s streaming sticks and comes with an Enhanced Voice Remote, so navigating apps and finding something to watch should feel familiar to anyone who already uses Roku.

LG’s 65-inch C6 OLED has the largest dollar discount in this sale at $1,350 off, which brings it from $2,699.99 down to $1,349.99.

There's no guarantee that Cyber Monday will bring lower TV prices, particularly when some of the Black Friday deals are already offering discounts approaching 50%. Retailers sometimes carry the same promotions through the entire shopping weekend, while others introduce new discounts or change which models are on sale.

That depends on your budget, room size, and how you plan to use it. The LG OLED evo C6 and Samsung S90H are worth considering for movie enthusiasts and gamers who want excellent contrast and smooth motion, while the Hisense U7 and TCL QM64L offer mini-LED alternatives for brighter living rooms. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If screen size is your priority, the 98-inch TCL F8D is also worth a look, provided you have the room for it.

Choosing between OLED and QLED is an important decision you need to ask yourself before you go shopping for TVs. If you can afford an OLED and want the best image possible, go for the OLED. Just make sure you're okay with the dimmer lights they emit. If you need brightness and don't want to blow out your budget on a TV, go with a QLED.

If you're seeing the deals on this post, they're real. But don't think every deal out there is real. Retailers are known to manipulate prices to make you think you're getting a better deal than you actually are. We vet our deals to make sure that doesn't happen, though.

#3283. The Wallet-Sized Xteink X4 Pro Is Lifehacker's E-Reader Gift of the Year, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

He continued, “I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance. Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3278. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Walmart appears to have dropped support for Apple Pay on its website and in its iPhone app. This comes just a few weeks after the retailer finally added support for Apple’s payment platform to its app and website.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Appleosophy spotted the change last week. There’s no indication whether the feature was removed deliberately or if this is some sort of bug.

Reolink’s 4K Solar Security Camera is down to $144.99 from $229.99, saving you $85. #3273. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

Update 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3270. Ariana Grande’s Best On-Screen Roles

Ariana Grande may be one of the biggest pop stars in the world, but she’s also a true multi-hyphenate, known for her uncanny impressions and acting chops. Grande can hit a killer vocal run, produce a sleek beat, and steal a scene with terrific comedic timing. (It’s called range.) Her Hollywood career has grown with her pop star status — she started as a Broadway baby, singing her heart out in the musical 13, and eventually became one of Nickelodeon’s most beloved airheads as she played Cat Valentine on Victorious.

Now, she’s starring alongside Robert De Niro in the new movie Focker-In-Law, which is out this week. So what better time to look back at the roles that have helped the megastar get to this point? Here are some of her most impressive moments both on the big and small screens.

Part of what makes Grande’s acting career so much fun to watch is that she never does what anyone is expecting her to do — and she’s not above extreme silliness. That makes her Zoolander 2 performance particularly entertaining. It’s extremely brief, but she pops on-screen just in time to have a wild orgy with Hansel (Owen Wilson). The scene marked her first time meeting Ben Stiller, who she reunites with in Focker-In-Law. She looked back at their meet-cute fondly during a recent appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon: “He was directing me in an orgy scene in Zoolander 2 with a hippo and Susan Sarandon,” she shared. “So right off the bat, we had a comfortability.” —Julyssa Lopez

Grande is one of the best parts of Adam McKay’s 2021 satire Don’t Look Up. She plays Riley Bina, a major pop star who is out-of-touch with the world — and the fact that a humanity-ending comet is headed Earth’s way. Once people start believing PhD student Kate Dibiasky (Jennifer Lawrence) and her advisor Dr. Randall Mindy (Leonardo DiCaprio) about their chilling prediction, Bina performs her new song “Just Look Up” with her cheating boyfriend, DJ Chello (Kid Cudi). The scene finds Grande delivering killer one-liners like, “Listen to the goddamn qualified scientists, we really fucked it up this time” while suspended onstage and sporting a ridiculous get-up of white feathers. According to McKay, many of the song’s lyrics were improvised by Grande. —Maya Georgi

In 2013, Nickelodeon adapted Gordon Korman’s 2008 novel Swindle, shaping it into a made-for-television heist movie revolving around two friends who set out to recover a $1.2 million baseball card. They form an unlikely group with other kids from their school harboring secret skills, and Grande steps in as a cheerleader with an undercover geeky side. The film came during her Sam & Cat days, and teamed her up with co-star Jennette McCurdy, while also letting her go beyond her flaky Cat persona. —J.L.

When Grande reprises the role of Glinda for the second half of the Wicked tale, she’s planning her wedding to Prince Fiyero, all of Emerald City idolizes her, and everything is as she always wished — or is it? As Glinda reevaluates her life and decides to change paths to help her friend Elphaba (Cynthia Erivo), there are fewer of the rollicking comedy moments that made Grande’s performance in the first film so fun to watch. But with big songs like “I Couldn’t Be Happier,” “The Girl in the Bubble,” and the booming duet “For Good,” she makes clear why she was a natural fit for the iconic role. —Kate Storey

Guest-starring on the campy horror-comedy television show Scream Queens as Chanel #2 was Ariana Grande’s first adult role after leaving Nickelodeon’s Sam & Cat to focus on her music. Creator Ryan Murphy said in 2015 that initially, Grande “was just going to do one episode, but she loved the process so much that she wanted to do more.” Even though she played a corpse in a few of those episodes, Ari’s comedic skills shine through, especially in a scene where her character’s ghost visits Emma Roberts’ Chanel #1. Grande is hilarious when speaking about her afterlife in hell. Whether her character is that she’s in a bad mood because Adolf Hitler was motorboating her boobs or that Jesus broke into heaven and stole the dinosaurs, she steals every scene. —Alison Weinflash

Let’s look beyond the fact that Cat Valentine seemingly has a legitimate lobotomy in the middle of the Victorious run. There would not be an Ariana Grande without the exposure, preparation, and genuine war stories that the cast ofVictorious went through. While the will-they-won’t-they nature of Cat’s relationship with Robbie (Matt Bennett) was finally resolved in the apocalyptic music video for “One Last Time,” the most memorable musical moments of the series all involved Grande: from the karaoke bar rendition of “Give it Up” to the “They didn’t say I couldn’t sing” riff on the Victorious iCarly collab “Leave It All to Shine.” As Cat, Grande earned her place in the Hollywood Arts High School hall of fame and started her path toward becoming a household name. —C.T. Jones

Ariana Grande has hosted SNL three times now, and she always makes her appearances memorable by leveraging her exceptional impersonation skills, showcasing her comedy agility, and refusing to shy away from being wildly silly. We’ve seen her play Jennifer Lawrence during a Family Feud recreation and playing a shy intern who saves her radio station with her ability to sound like everyone from Shakira to Celine Dion. But her most beloved contributions might be in an off-key bridesmaid in the famed Domingo skit and giving us a hilarious take on Home Alone. —J.L.

Grande’s character in Focker In Law, Olivia Jones, is a multi-hyphenate not unlike the actress who portrays her. Just swap the gold records for FBI credentials, throw in vegan cooking chops, and you have a future in-law (to grandpa Jack Byrnes, reprised brilliantly by Robert De Niro) hell-bent on entering the “circle of trust” in record time. Grande plays the ultra-competitive Liv with exacting comedic timing, offering the perfect foil for Ben Stiller’s goofball insecurity. —Shirley Halperin

It takes self-determination, drive, and a lot of pink to make the world’s most coveted role your own. Ariana Grande wasn’t the frontrunner when Universal first announced it would be making a Wicked film. But the Petal singer fought to claim Glinda’s glitter wand. “Oz has been my safe space for as long as I can remember,” she wrote in an open letter to fans before the film’s premiere. It’s hard to imagine a world where the gleeful shrieks of Grande’s “Popular” outro didn’t exist — and her participation in the John M. Chu duology is a career-defining moment, proof the former Nick star is never far from her musical theater roots. —C.T.J.

#3269. ‘Saint-Pierre’ Season 3 Trailer Sees New Faces Shake Up Life For Fitz & Arch

EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Season 3 of this week’s Global Breakout, Saint-Pierre.

The CBC drama series, which stars Allan Hawco and Jósephine Jobert as a cop duo on a small island off Newfoundland, is returning to Canadian screens on January 4, 2027, and we’ve got a first video for the new season.

We’ve also got some new information on Season 3, which we’ll keep vague to avoid spoilers on previous seasons. The story begins with Jobert’s Acting Chief of the SPMP Geneviève Archambault (Arch) and Royal Newfoundland Constabulary Inspector Donald Fitzpatrick (Fitz) racing to keep the peace on the France-administered Saint-Pierre as a gang war erupts. Related Stories News 'Saint-Pierre' Is The High-Rating Canadian Cop Series Proving Small Island Life Can Provide The Drama Trailers 'Bunker' Trailer: Penélope Cruz & Javier Bardem Clash In Florian Zeller's Venice Breakout; UK Release Date Set

An organized crime expert, Pascal Lalonde (Assaad Bouab), is sent from Paris as the new police chief and his presence destabilizes Arch professionally and personally, with the pair sharing a previous connection. “What kind of Wild West cop shop have you been running?” he asks her just before the trailer cuts to a deceased young woman covered head to toe in a clay-like substance being lifted out of a trunk. Watch on Deadline

As an aside, Bouab played a Saint-Pierre bartender in Peaky Blinders in a storyline about smuggling channels, though those scenes were shot in Manchester, UK, meaning this was his first time on the island. Saint-Pierre is shot on location.

Season 3 will also introduce mysterious businesswoman Victoria Peters, who arrives on the island with a vision to make it a top tourist destination and instantly has an intense chemistry with Fitz. French-Canadian actress Caroline Dhavernas is playing the character.

Saint-Pierre‘s third season runs to 12 episodes. Hawco Productions is back to produce for CBC and streamer CBC Gem, with Fifth Season once again handling international distribution. Outside of Canada, the show goes out on Sky in New Zealand, Disney+ across Eastern Europe and Belgium, ABC in Australia, FreeTV in Israel, BBC Studios in the Netherlands and Poland, and on U&Alibi in the UK, and France Télévisions.

Given its big ratings in Canada, where it became CBC‘s most popular show in the 2025/26 season and among the most watched across Canada, we selected it as our Global Breakout this week. Fifth Season has struck a slew of deals, but has not sold it into the U.S. yet.

Hawco – who writes, produces and stars in the show – told us this week: “We’re super happy with how it has been performing in Canada… We’ve also been doing very well internationally, and it’s only a matter of time before we find the right home in the U.S. market. Our partner Fifth Season leads the way in sales outside Canada, and I know they’ve been very selective about where that home should be.”

Hawco is the show’s co-creator alongside Robina Lord-Stafford.

#3268. 2026 tech gift guide for Apple users

Black Friday week is here, so it’s officially time to start checking gifts off your list. For my 2026 tech gift guide, I’m recommending technology products that I’ve personally used all year. Each of these products has been especially useful this year, and they’ll make great gifts for the Apple users in your life.

$1,199.00 (reg. $1,499.00) for the current M5 model with 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage

I love my 15-inch MacBook Air. It has room for multiple windows without overlapping and is still thin and light enough to carry around. The Sky Blue finish looks great next to my Glacier iPhone 18 Pro, too.

13-inch M5 iPad Pro (512GB, Wi-Fi, Silver, standard glass) — $1,349.00 (reg. $1,699.00)Apple Pencil Pro — $99.00 (reg. $129.00)

Some weekends I unwind by casually sketching with my iPad Pro and Apple Pencil Pro in Procreate. Other times I get lost in a TV show. The deep blacks on the OLED display really stand out in dark scenes and dark rooms. It’s the nicest screen I own.

$39.99 (reg. $49.99) for the 11-inch iPad Pro (M4 and M5) kit

If you’re giving an iPad and Apple Pencil to someone who likes to sketch, I’d add Astropad’s Rock Paper Pencil 4.0. The matte screen protector gives the Pencil more drag and clings to the display without adhesive, so you can peel it off when you want the glossy screen back. The kit comes with two graphite-style tips for sketching and two smoother ballpoint tips for taking notes.

AirPods Pro 3 are the earbuds I use daily. Apple rates them for up to eight hours of listening on a charge with noise cancellation on, and sound quality is unmatched for their size and price.

$699.99 (reg. $799.00) for the 49mm Natural Titanium case with the Translucent Gray Ocean Band

Battery life is a big reason I wear an Ultra. Apple rates the Ultra 4 for up to 50 hours of normal use, so I can leave it on overnight to track my sleep. My favorite change this year is the live heart rate complication. It updates every five seconds and fits in one small spot on the watch face, freeing up the whole row I used to give it.

The current Beats Pill is my go-to Bluetooth speaker. Beats rates it for up to 24 hours on a charge. Matte Black is the one on sale, and it comes in plenty of other colors.

$14.00 (reg. $34.99) for two five-foot cables · $18.99 for one

If your car has a USB-A port for wired CarPlay and your iPhone has USB-C, these woven Beats cables connect the two. Plug one in and you get Maps and music on the dashboard while your iPhone charges. The two-pack costs less than a single cable this week.

CarlinKit Mini Ultra 3 — $35.99Twelve South AirFly Drive — $31.99 (reg. $39.99)

These are for cars that already have wired CarPlay. Plug either adapter into the USB port you’d normally use for your iPhone and pair it once. After that, CarPlay connects wirelessly when you get in, so your phone can stay in your pocket. The CarlinKit Mini Ultra 3 is one of my favorite stocking stuffers, and Twelve South’s AirFly Drive is $4 less this week.

AirTag (second generation) — $18.00 (reg. $29.00) for oneBelkin Secure Holder with Key Ring — $9.99 (reg. $12.95)

I’d give these two together to someone who’s always looking for their keys on the way out the door. If they’re somewhere in the house, you can make the AirTag chime in Find My. A compatible iPhone can also point you toward the keys as you get closer.

$23.20 (reg. $29.00) with Prime, in white

It took losing my wallet twice to convince me to put a tracker in it. Nomad’s Tracking Card fits in a regular card slot, and I can make it ring from Find My. When the card needs a charge, I put it on the same MagSafe charger I use for my iPhone.

$89.99 (reg. $139.99) with Prime, in blue

When my kids’ iPads are running low during use, I grab the UGREEN Nexode Pro power bank. One USB-C cable pulls out of the pack and the other doubles as the carrying strap. It has a capacity of 25,000mAh, which lasts long enough to actually be useful.

The Belkin 3-in-1 stand I recommended last year still lives on my nightstand. At bedtime, my iPhone snaps onto MagSafe, my Apple Watch goes on the puck when I’m not sleep tracking, and my AirPods charge on the pad underneath.

UGREEN MagFlow Air — $52.24 (reg. $79.99) with PrimeINIU SnapGo Air — $46.74 (reg. $54.99)Aulumu M10 — $71.98 (reg. $89.98) with the Amazon coupon

The UGREEN MagFlow Air is handy on days when I need my iPhone to last longer. It’s a 10,000mAh battery that’s slim enough to leave on my iPhone when I slip it into my pocket.

If your iPhone supports 25W wireless charging, I’d go with the INIU SnapGo Air. It also holds 10,000mAh and costs the least of the three.

For an overnight trip, I’d bring the Aulumu M10. My iPhone snaps onto one side, and the Apple Watch charging puck on the back means I can leave my watch cable at home.

$87.99 (reg. $109.99) for 55- to 65-inch TVs

My family loves seeing the colors in a movie spill onto the wall behind the TV. The Govee TV Backlight 3 uses a small camera to match the lights behind the TV to what’s on screen. It works whether we’re watching through Apple TV, a gaming console, or using one of the TV’s built-in apps.

Matic bundle — $1,495.00 (reg. $1,795.00)Matic Serene bundle — $1,595.00 (reg. $2,095.00)Both offers run through December 1.

Matic is hands-down the most fun and reliable robot mop/vac combo. Matic added Apple Home support through Matter this year, so I can ask Siri to start cleaning. I can also say “Hey Matic, mop the kitchen” directly to the robot using its Gemini-powered voice controls.

Sink Summon is still one of my favorite features. If Matic runs out of water in the middle of a clean, it rolls over to the spot I marked by the sink. I fill the tank, close the lid, and it picks up where it left off. The new Matic Serene is even quieter, and existing owners can reserve a paid upgrade to get the quieter hardware in the Matic they already have.

$899.00 (reg. $1,299.00) at BowFlex through November 27

This year, Apple GymKit at home became affordable thanks to the BowFlex T6 treadmill. GymKit shows my heart rate on the console and sends the treadmill’s distance and incline back to my Apple Watch. The dials on the grips might be my favorite part. I roll the right one to pick up the pace or the left one to raise the incline without breaking stride.

I keep the Withings BeamO in the medicine cabinet. It puts a contactless thermometer and a digital stethoscope in one handheld device. Rather than being intimidating, my kids think it’s fun to use — even when they don’t feel well. The Withings app saves temperatures and recordings of heart and lung sounds, with separate profiles so a household can share it.

Birdbuddy Pro Solar’s camera takes photos and video when a bird stops by, and the solar roof helps keep it charged between visits. I always look forward to opening a postcard on my iPhone to see who came for lunch. The person you give it to can get those postcards with a free Birdbuddy account, without paying for a subscription.

2 Mini — $99.99 (reg. $149.99) with Prime2 Pro — $199.99 (reg. $299.99) with Prime

I also like how both Kiwibit feeders look. The Mini’s 4K camera captures a lot of detail for such a small feeder. I’d go with the full-size Pro for autofocus and slow motion. At one-eighth speed, you can see what a bird does with its wings just before its feet touch the perch.

Overall, I prefer the notifications in the Birdbuddy app. They do a better job of telling me about the visits, but the two Kiwibit options are great hardware with useful apps as well.

To set up the ANTHBOT M9, I steered it around the edge of the lawn with my iPhone and marked the tree roots I wanted it to avoid. That gave the mower a map to follow without having to bury a perimeter wire. Now I get to hang out in the yard with my dog, Nova, while the mower cuts the grass. It’s quiet enough that she barely pays attention to it. It’s saved me a ton of yard hours this year, letting me focus on spending more time with family.
