#3212. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

Rats don't hibernate during the winter months, instead they desperately seek out warm shelter. And while there's one thing you should clear from your yard to prevent rats, you should also be focused on your shed.

It's the perfect spot for rats to take up residence and once they find somewhere they like, they'll stick around and populate. So, before you end up with a rat infestation in your shed, here's the 3 things I recommend doing every winter to make sure they stay out (and stay away from your home, too).

Rats can fit into holes as small as a quarter, so if you've got any gaps around your shed, they'll be sure to find a way in. And if they don't find an appropriate hole, they might chew one of their own to gain access. So, what I like to do every winter is a thorough check of the exterior and interior of my shed looking for any holes.

If you find any, it also matters what you seal the gap with, as they may just break their way through something too flimsy.

For this, I recommend using a steel wool or wire mesh. If you notice they're digging underneath, it might also be worth laying some concrete slabs or gravel around these areas, too.

Steel wool is great for filling holes and blocking gaps around your shed. Then, the rats won't be able to chew through, creating the perfect barrier to keep them out. It can be used for both indoor and outdoor filling and can be easily cut to size with scissors. With this 2-Pack, you'll get 3" x 10ft coverage.

The problem with rats moving into your shed is that once they're there, you'll likely need to call in pest control to get them out. If you try and deal with it yourself by going in and moving things around, you might encourage the rats to move towards your home and into your garden instead.

To prevent this, I like to give my shed a good sort out before winter to make sure there's no places for the rats to hide.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I like to grab a few plastic boxes with lids to store anything in that I might have been leaving discarded on the floor and, if you've got space, shelves are also great for moving things off the floor and keeping them away from gnawing teeth.

While storing any seeds, bulbs or bird food in your shed seems like a good idea, it's not so true in winter. As well as looking for shelter, rats are also looking for food. So, if you have seeds and a shed, they'll more than happily move in.

What I like to do is move all the seeds and anything else the rats might want to eat out of my shed and seal them away inside my home instead. But, if you don't have room, putting these things into stainless steel containers with screw-on lids and leaving them in your shed will keep them away from rats.

With these three simple steps, I've avoided rats year-in-year-out and, hopefully, you will too. Fortunately, doing these tasks is also super affordable and will cost you far less to carry out than calling in pest control.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3203. Trump’s “Noisy Name-Calling” Mocked By NYT After Bored POTUS Starts Thanksgiving Ranting Against Reporter’s Nvidia Dispatch

Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics

Like death and taxes, you can always rely on there being an annoying relative at the table on Thanksgiving, and you can always depend on Donald Trump losing his marbles on Turkey Day.

Down in his Florida compound (which no one but Trump calls the Southern White House), the former Apprentice host took time early this AM local time to go on social media to blast off about the New York Times‘ reporting on Nvidia and the reinstating of scandal plagued CEO Jensen Huang. As well as likely keeping aide Natalie Harp busy posting for him, Trump pleaded with Vladimir Putin to “pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” approving disaster relief for parts of the Sunshine State, boasting about the state of the economy and his extensive and pricey White House redecorations. Related Stories News Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day News Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL's First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton

However, with the possible of that last topic, Trump’s real vigor seemed to be reserved for chastising the Gray Lady and veteran journalist David Sanger. Watch on Deadline

Trump termed Sanger as a “mediocre reporter” after the Times ran a piece bylined by him on Trump’s much bragged about direct role in Huang rejoining the AI chip company he founded. Stinging Trump likely more, Sanger also wrote about the lack of stock market success that Huang’s return has brought Nivida, a company POTUS owns millions in stock in. Revealing his thin skin, Trump went on to say: “David Sanger is a lowlife that only writes what he is told to write by his bosses. Also, until the Election, best Market, EVER, 82 days, settled 8 Wars, and the USA is respected again like never before!”

Having had some success of late in Florida courts against the NYT in a $15 billion defamation suit, Trump had to , as he so often does, list off his assumed accomplishments — many of which are questionable to put it nicely.

In their own way, the Times were equally blunt and all-incompassing in their response today.

“If readers want to understand the market effects of President Trump’s interventions, including Nvidia’s reversal, his disruption of international trade, and his decision to go to war with Iran, then David Sanger’s latest report is an essential read,” the Ochs-Sulzberger family-owned outlet said this Thanksgiving Day. The NYT added: “David has covered five American presidents in more than four decades at The Times; his coverage of the ways in which the administration is shaping foreign policy and national security is unmatched. Noisy name-calling is just an attempt to distract from the news.”

That last line kinda sums up this second Trump administration, and the first, in PR poetry.

#3202. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 During Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3201. Major MacBook Air ‘overhaul’ could launch next year, per Gurman

Apple has a new MacBook Air with M6 chip coming early next year, but per Mark Gurman on his latest podcast episode, a “big MacBook Air overhaul” could launch as early as 2027 too. Here’s what he said.

Today on the latest episode of Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the well-sourced reporter answered a listener question that involves the future of the MacBook Air.

When asked about the next-generation MacBook Air, here’s what Gurman said:

The next MacBook Air project, J913 and J915, the 13-inch version and the 15-inch version, that is coming in spring 2027 alongside the MacBook Neo 2. And this is going to be another “chip and ship,” so a chip refresh.

And we are getting to the end of the road here for the current MacBook Air design. The current MacBook Air design was introduced in ’22, was refreshed in ’23 with the 15-inch model. We’re now in 2027. MacBook Air is Apple’s most popular computer, and they need to keep it very fresh. And so my anticipation is 2027-2028 is when we’re going to get the big MacBook Air overhaul. And I think OLED will be part of that conversation.

There are several noteworthy takeaways here:

It would be unusual for Apple to launch two distinct MacBook Air models in the same calendar year. However, if that does happen, it would follow the exact same playbook Apple used with the MacBook Pro this year.

This March, a new MacBook Pro launched with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips but the same design that’s been around since 2021. Then in October, Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display and a new industrial design.

It sounds like a very similar rollout could happen for the MacBook Air in 2027.

You can watch Mark Gurman’s latest podcast episode below.

Are you interested in a redesigned MacBook Air with OLED? Let us know in the comments.

#3200. The Oura Ring 5 Is $100 Off During Black Friday Sales

The Oura Ring 5 is the world’s smallest smart ring and looks more like a piece of stylish jewelry than a fitness tracker. Though it’s rarely discounted, it’s currently seeing a record-low price of $299 (originally $399) in this early Black Friday deal.

In addition to being 40% smaller than its predecessor, the Oura Ring 5 also lasts up to nine days longer than the Oura Ring 4, and has upgraded sensors for better accuracy. It’s completely waterproof and more durable, with increased scratch resistance, but still has the same discreet aesthetic, with a titanium build. It earned an Editors’ Choice Award from PCMag and has new features like long-term breathing-pattern measurements and overnight blood-pressure checks, joining the suite of features that track sleep, health, and activity trends.

It does charge an annual membership fee to access most of those features, so those looking for a basic fitness tracker might want to opt for a cheaper alternative like the Fitbit Air. However, if you’re shopping for a more robust screen-less health and fitness tracker with an exceptional, elegant design that feels lightweight and looks natural,  the Oura Ring 5 is a worthwhile option.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. #3196. Jesse Eisenberg Says “There’s No Sexuality To My Work” & Why Life Is “Different” When Fans “Want To Sleep With A Person Onscreen”

Jesse Eisenberg is reflecting on his work in Hollywood and why he has a very different experience with fans in public than some other actors.

In a new interview with The New Yorker, the actor, director, writer, and producer of The Debut said fans of his work are “mostly fine” when they see him in public, as his roles are not sexualized.

Eisenberg said in the interview that he goes to the New York Public Library, where he writes scripts. When asked if people interrupt him when they recognize who he is, he told the publication, “People are mostly fine.” Related Stories News Jesse Eisenberg TV Series Produced By Peter Rice To Be Taken Out By A24 News Jesse Eisenberg Reveals Thoughts On 'The Social Reckoning' & Why He Turned Down Zuckerberg Role

“It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he added. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.” Watch on Deadline

Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar for his role in Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, recalled an interaction with a fan.

“I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he said. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.”

The actor didn’t return for the sequel, The Social Reckoning, and has been outspoken about his decision. Succession alum Jeremy Strong took on the role of Zuckerberg after Eisenberg declined.

Eisenberg’s The Debut opens in theaters on December 11, and the cast also includes Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halley Bailey, Colton Ryan, and Bernadette Peters, among others.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There comes a point on Thanksgiving when the kids are getting restless, dinner is still an hour away and everyone has run out of things to talk about. Believe it or not, ChatGPT might be the most entertaining guest at your Thanksgiving gathering.

While you've probably heard that the chatbot can help you plan your menu, figure out how long to cook a turkey and come up with creative ways to use leftovers, some of my favorite ways to use ChatGPT have absolutely nothing to do with cooking.

From hosting a family game show to creating an interactive holiday mystery or even building a playable video game in seconds, ChatGPT can bring the whole family together in some surprisingly creative ways.

So, before everyone retreats to their phones or falls asleep on the couch, here are five ChatGPT prompts to keep the whole family entertained this Thanksgiving.

When you're done with the board games, you can turn ChatGPT into a game show host. All you need is to use Voice Mode to have the chatbot read questions aloud, keep track of scores and announce the winner.

The fun part is that you can tailor the questions to the people in the room. Mix Thanksgiving trivia with pop culture, general knowledge and funny facts about your family.

Try this prompt: Act as an energetic game show host for our Thanksgiving gathering. Create five rounds of questions that appeal to both kids and adults, including Thanksgiving trivia, pop culture, riddles and silly challenges. Ask one question at a time, let us answer and keep track of each team's score. Include a dramatic final round.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

If you've already taken the obligatory Thanksgiving family photo, upload it to ChatGPT and have a little fun with it.

Ask ChatGPT to reimagine everyone as characters in an '80s sitcom, passengers aboard the Mayflower or royalty attending an extravagant medieval feast. You could even turn your family into the stars of a fictional Thanksgiving movie.

Let everyone take turns choosing a theme and vote on the funniest result. You might end up with something worth framing.

Try this prompt: Transform this family photo into a hilariously dramatic 1980s sitcom promotional poster for a fictional Thanksgiving special. Give everyone period-appropriate outfits, exaggerated expressions and big hairstyles while preserving their recognizable facial features. Come up with a funny title for the show.

Who stole Grandma's pumpkin pie? Why has the turkey mysteriously disappeared? And why is Uncle Bob suddenly refusing to answer questions?

ChatGPT can create an interactive mystery game in which everyone at the table becomes a detective. Unlike a traditional mystery game, the chatbot can respond to your questions and introduce new clues as you play.

You can customize the difficulty depending on who's participating and keep the mystery lighthearted if younger children want to join in.

Try this prompt: Create an interactive, family-friendly Thanksgiving mystery called "The Case of the Missing Pumpkin Pie." Introduce five suspicious fictional characters, each with a motive and a secret. Let us investigate by questioning suspects and examining evidence. Keep the culprit a secret until we make our final accusation. Make the mystery solvable in about 15 minutes.

One of the most entertaining things you can do with ChatGPT is build your own simple browser-based game without knowing how to code.

And Thanksgiving lends itself to some wonderfully ridiculous ideas. Imagine a game in which a turkey has to escape the dinner table, a pumpkin pie falls from the sky or a player has to dodge flying Brussels sprouts.

Have everyone contribute an idea, then ask ChatGPT to combine them into a playable game. Depending on your ChatGPT interface, you may be able to preview it directly or save the generated HTML file and open it in a web browser.

Try this prompt: Build a playable browser game called "The Great Thanksgiving Escape." The player controls a turkey trying to escape a kitchen while dodging flying vegetables and collecting pumpkin pies for bonus points. Include colorful retro arcade graphics, keyboard and touchscreen controls, a high score and a restart button. Make everything work in a single HTML file with no external dependencies.

This might be my favorite idea because it could lead to conversations you wouldn't otherwise have around the dinner table.

Ask ChatGPT to host a personalized version of a "Most Likely To" game or a family edition of The Newlywed Game. Everyone writes down their answers before revealing them, and the person with the most matching answers wins.

The questions can be funny, nostalgic or completely unexpected. Just keep them away from anything that might reignite an old family argument. ChatGPT can help entertain your relatives, but there's only so much it can do about Thanksgiving drama.

Try this prompt: Host a funny, heartwarming game of "How Well Do You Know Your Family?" for our Thanksgiving gathering. Give us 20 questions, one at a time, that encourage us to guess each other's answers. Include childhood memories, favorite foods, funny habits and ridiculous hypothetical situations. Keep everything lighthearted and appropriate for all ages.

So much of the conversation around AI focuses on how it can help us get more done and be more productive. But one of the things I enjoy most about ChatGPT is experimenting with what it can do when there's absolutely nothing I need to accomplish.

This Thanksgiving, rather than disappearing into your phone while everyone else scrolls through theirs, try using ChatGPT to get everyone laughing, talking or playing something together. Who knows, you might just start a new Thanksgiving tradition.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to plan around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a big step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a new Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

At the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

There comes a point when your child is old enough to potentially get their own Kindle, mostly so they stop stealing yours and filling up your library with Big Nate collections.

Now is the perfect time to find the right Kindle for your child, as Amazon typically puts many of its Kindles on sale for Black Friday. You may not have known that Amazon has kid versions of the Kindle, Paperwhite and Colorsoft.

Unfortunately, none of them are on sale, and in general they're more expensive than their "adult" counterparts. But Amazon also offers a bit more out of the box with the kid versions.

Let's break down what you get with the Kid Kindle and why the higher price may be worth it.

To be up front, as far as we can tell, the different Kindle Kids eReaders are the same hardware that you get with the standard Kindle, Paperwhite and Colorsoft.

The difference is that the Kid version comes with a case included. Right now, the Paperwhite Kids can be purchased with the Pirate theme, "Bookman," or Lakeside Retreat.

Additionally, the Kid Kindles come with a 1-year Kids+ subscription included. Basically, this is a more curated version of Kindle Plus (the rebranded of Kindle Unlimited) for children. It includes thousands of books for kids ages 6 through 12, like the Percy Jackson series or Diary of a Wimpy Kid. Also, the Kid version does not come with ads or distractions.

The Kid Kindles also have parent controls that can be accessed through the Parent Dashboard mobile app which can be used to suggest books or set screen limits.

Amazon updated most of its Kindle lineup earlier this year, but the 2024 version of the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is still available and the only Kids eReader on sale at $149. This version comes with 16GB of storage, a case, 6 months of Amazon Kids+, and a waterproof design.

By comparison, the adult Kindles do not come with a case, only three months of Kindle+ (which adds a cost), and you have to choose ad-supported or without lockscreen ads (again more expensive).

There are content controls and parent controls on normal Kindles, but in my experience, it's more finicky and usually requires a separate account if you truly want to lock things down. Quite annoying when you're sharing with your child and your wife is filling the library with romantasy novels. Not yet, buddy, not yet.

Both the kids and adult versions can be used to access library books through the Libby app, literally the best thing about Kindles compared to most other eReaders.

Here's the big difference: price. Let's use the Kindle Paperwhite as our example.

The Ad-free, 3-month Kindle+, Paperwhite costs $219 when its not on sale. The ad-supported version costs $199. The new Kids Kindle Paperwhite costs $229.

For a less expensive option, the cheapest standard Kindle is $149, while the Kids version costs $179. The case adds up the Kids version, but if you want a case for the adult version, the cheapest one I saw on Amazon tacks on $21 to the price.

If money isn't as big of a concern, the Kids Kindle Colorsoft is $299 but is great for kids who starting to read comic books or if you want the option for color stories. The base adult Colorsoft starts at $289 but there is a bundle with a case for $301, which is on sale.

Amazon refreshed the Kids Kindle this year with a thinner and lighter version. It features a 6-inch glare-free display, a themed case, and 1-year of Kids+ subscription. The Kids Kindle has up to 6 weeks of battery life and you can listen to audio books using Bluetooth headphones. Parents can control settings with the Parent dashboard.

The big difference is that I rarely see the Kid versions go on sale while the standard Kindles get discounted throughout the year typically around Black Friday, the new Spring sale and the big Prime Day summer sale.

Also, the subscription. You get three months of Kindle+ which normally costs $11.99 per month (or $143.88) for a year. The Kid Kindle comes with 12 months of Kids+, which normally costs $7.99 a month for Prime Members or $8.99 if you don't have an account.

Additionally, if you have other Amazon devices like the Amazon Kids Echo or an Amazon Kids tablet, your Kids+ subscription is accessible across each device with a child profile.

The upfront costs of the Kid Kindle is higher in general, but over the first year, if you keep the subscription, you're paying on par with the adult Kindle and getting more control and curation.

As we noted above, you don't have to get the newest model and Amazon has done a decent job of supporting much older Kindles.

In this case, don't let the sticker shock get to you and consider the Kindle Kid, Kindle Paperwhite Kid, or Kindle Colorsoft Kid for your child.

There's no better time to buy a Garmin watch than the Black Friday sales, because it's almost always the period you'll find the lowest prices available on any Garmin.

This year the sale is especially good, because not only have excellent older Garmin watches like the Forerunner 265 and Forerunner 965 returned to their lowest-ever price, but the latest Garmin watches like the Fenix 9 and Forerunner 170 have also been significantly discounted for the first time.

I've been testing Garmin watches for a decade and I think the only watch I can't find a deal on right now is the Enduro 4, but even there you don't have to worry, because the almost equally good Enduro 3 is down to $699 at Amazon.

I’ve picked out 17 deals on the best Garmin watches available right now, from cheaper Forerunner models all the way up to the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, which is $849 in the Amazon sale and still a better buy than the Fenix 9 in the sale, in my opinion.

I think the Forerunner 70 is the best beginner running watch available, and it actually has all the features runners of all levels really need. It's accurate and comfortable to wear 24/7 thanks to its small design, and this is the first time it's dropped under $200 on sale.

The Forerunner 165 is the predecessor to the Forerunner 70 and Forerunner 170 watches, and a good pick, especially for new runners. This is one of the few Garmin deals I'm a little disappointed by this Black Friday, though, because the Forerunner 165 has dropped as low as $129 in the past.

The Forerunner 170 has a few extra features compared to the Forerunner 70, most notably music storage, and also comes in this delightful teal color ( which I'd say makes it worth the upgrade alone). It's a great running watch and is getting its first big discounts this Black Friday.

This is the biggest percentage discount I've seen on a Garmin watch right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED a strong, adventurous alternative to the Fenix and Enduro. It offers incredible battery life and a distinctive, rugged design, as well as reliable sports tracking, but it does lack the maps you get on pricier models.

This is one of the best deals going on for a Garmin right now, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display. It even comes in two sizes and I'd say the only watch that can rival it for this price is the Coros Pace 4.

The Vivoactive 6 is an attractive smartwatch with impressive sports tracking credentials. It has dropped as low as $229 in the past, so a better deal might be yet to come on the watch this Black Friday, but this is still a good price on a well-rounded watch.

The Forerunner 965 is the best alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix lineup if you're looking for value this Black Friday. It has brilliant sports tracking and navigation features, and a thin, lightweight design. You'll be hard-pressed to find a better watch from any brand for $449.

The Garmin Venu 4 combines its attractive, smartwatch-style design with Garmin's excellent sports tracking, and even as a marathoner, I prefer it to the more sports-focused Forerunner 570, partly because it has a built-in flashlight.

I don't think the Forerunner 570 offers better value than the Venu 4 or Forerunner 965 at the same price, but it does have some more striking design options than those watches, which might tempt you ot pick it up instead. It's a great sports tracker, of course, but lacks maps and a flashlight.

The Venu X1 stands out from other Garmins thanks to its ultra-thin design, but even though it looks like a smartwatch, it's actually packed with the same brilliant sports and navigation features as you get on the Forerunner 970. At $300 off, it might be the sleeper hit of the sales.

The Epix Pro is the value alternative to the latest Fenix watches, but I'm a little disappointed it hasn't dropped to a lower price than this, because it has been as cheap as $499 in the past.

I rate the Garmin Forerunner 970 as the best overall sports watch on the market, so getting any kind of discount on it is welcome, and this is a return to the lowest price it's ever been available. It has all of Garmin's top sports tracking and training analysis features, plus maps, all in a lightweight, durable design.

This is a good price for a great adventure watch if you prefer a MIP display, but the fact that the Fenix 7 Pro has been superseded by three rounds of Fenixes at this point makes me hope there might still be better deals to come. If not, this is still worth looking at as the cheapest titanium Garmin watch with maps and a MIP display on sale.

I've just tested the Garmin Enduro 4 and I'd say the Enduro 3 is the better value buy for sure, because it has all the same key features as the new watch for $200 less on sale. Those features include the longest battery life of any Garmin, thanks to the Enduro 4's MIP display and solar panels.

The Fenix 8 has now been superseded by the Fenix 8 Pro and Fenix 9, but I think it's still worth considering because it's cheaper than those watches on sale. You don't get the connectivity features available on newer Fenixes, but otherwise the Fenix 8 matches up well with regard to its core features, and it's also a little thinner than the new models.

The new Fenix 9 Pro has a few upgrades over the Fenix 8 Pro, including an all-titanium case, and is also on sale, but the Fenix 8 Pro is still a savvier buy thanks to this $350 saving, in my opinion. It has LTE and satellite connectivity on top of its outstanding sports tracking and navigation features, and is $150 less than the Fenix 9 Pro right now on sale.

All models of the Garmin Fenix 9 are reduced by at least $100 for Black Friday, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro with InReach, which is the watch I'm using as my main tracker right now. If you want the latest and greatest Garmin watch, this is the time to buy it, because it's the first time it's been discounted anywhere.
