#3157. Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the company responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the company can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

Apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:

“The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed new (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s new restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”

As for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”

Arguments by the Little Tech Association, AAI, Public Knowledge, and the EFF all follow a similar line, with some also addressing how Apple’s restrictions on external payment links could affect consumer choice, pricing, and competition.

Here’s the full list of parties that filed amicus briefs in support of Epic Games:

What’s your take on these briefs? Let us know in the comments.

#3156. Firms set up memory chip ‘war rooms’ as some prices jump 10x, WSJ reports

The memory chip shortage has staff trawling eBay and brokers for a handful of chips. Even Elon Musk got no special deal from Samsung’s chairman, according to a second-hand account.

Electronics makers have set up procurement “war rooms” to hunt for memory chips. Prices for some chips have risen tenfold in a year, Jiyoung Sohn and Sooyoung Rhee reported for The Wall Street Journal. Staff scour eBay, call hundreds of brokers and buy batches as small as five to 12 units, the newspaper found.

Smaller firms are hit hardest. Large buyers can lock in supply through long-term deals with the chipmakers. Others rely on brokers and the grey market. Some sellers there mix used chips into orders of new ones, the Journal reported.

“Suddenly, I’ll hear a string of bad language and ask what’s going on,” Blackmagic Design chief executive Grant Petty told the Journal.

Taiwanese memory module maker Apacer has taken out loans so it has cash ready whenever supply appears, according to the report.

“If chips show up, we take it. This is crazy, but there is no other way,” Apacer president Gibson Chen told the Journal.

Thieves took about $100,000 of flash memory from one company’s warehouse in Indonesia, the paper reported. The firm suspects a former employee.

The Journal also carried a second-hand account of a meeting between Elon Musk and Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong. Capital Group’s Carl Kawaja said Musk told him about it in June. Musk asked for a long-term memory deal, and Lee replied that everyone offers that.

“We get that offer from everyone. What else can you do for us?” Lee asked, according to Kawaja’s account.

Musk then offered to guarantee financing for a new Samsung chip plant, Kawaja said, and got the same answer. TNW has not independently verified the account. Sam Altman has also courted the company, meeting Samsung’s presidents in October.

The shortage comes as Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron move production to the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. SK Hynix has said tight supply could last until 2030.

Consumers are already paying. In India, around 48 Samsung and Xiaomi phone models went up by ₹1,000 to ₹4,000 in mid-November, Inc42 reported. Samsung’s Galaxy A07 5G now costs ₹22,999, up from ₹20,999.

AI start-ups are feeling it in the cloud. GPU rental prices in India have risen 30% to 35% since February, Subhashish Banerjee, co-founder of Bharat1 AI, told Inc42. Providers now want three to six month commitments from start-ups that once booked a few hours at a time.

Some are cutting their needs instead. SquadStack, which runs voice AI agents, built smaller models trained on its own call data. Fewer tokens per call cut its costs even as hardware got pricier, chief executive Apurv Agrawal told Inc42. Memory costs have also hit Xiaomi’s quarterly profit and Apple’s margins.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. #3153. 1Password confirms security incident, here’s what you need to know

Password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its users, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

According to the company, the incident began on November 19, when it started investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The company noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our users,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That said, the company confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The company also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Finally, 1Password said users do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

#3151. Binance fully reopens withdrawals nearly a month after its $6.3B hack

Binance withdrawals are open again across almost every network. The exchange says it covered the stolen assets with $6.34 billion of its own money, while the hackers keep moving funds.

Richard Teng, then Binance’s head of regional markets, at Binance Blockchain Week 2023 in Istanbul.

Binance has lifted the last of the withdrawal limits it put in place after its record $6.3 billion hack in October. The exchange said on Thursday that its withdrawal recovery work is complete.

“Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted,” Binance said.

A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance or planned upgrades. Binance said those pauses cover a very small share of normal traffic and are separate from the recovery.

Binance halted withdrawals after the breach on 29 October and began restoring them on 1 November, starting with Bitcoin. Deposits stayed open throughout, crypto.news reported.

The first day brought a rush. Customers took out $4.65 billion and put in $1.01 billion in the first nine and a half hours on 1 November, the exchange said. That left a net outflow of $3.64 billion. Binance reopened 87 more networks in the week to 14 November.

The exchange has said it covered the stolen assets with more than $6.34 billion of its own money. It drew on its corporate treasury, part of its user protection fund and part of its futures insurance fund. It has pledged to rebuild the user fund to about $1 billion, and published a reserve snapshot covering 198 tokens.

Wallets linked to the hack moved another $35.52 million in Ether on Thursday, according to blockchain tracker Onchain Lens. It put the hackers’ remaining unfrozen holdings at about $1.9 billion.

US authorities and private companies have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen crypto. The Justice Department also won court approval to seize more than $1.2 billion of it, The Block reported on 12 November.

The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the theft. Binance said a fake job interview gave the attackers their way in. Days after the hack, the exchange insisted it was in ‘very strong’ health.

#3148. Wispr Flow improves dictation accuracy with new Canto-2 speech-to-text model

Popular AI dictation app Wispr Flow is rolling out a new speech-to-text model for Mac, iPhone, and other platforms, promising fewer transcription errors and better recognition of names and technical terms. Here are the details.

Wispr Flow this week launched Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the company says reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

In practice, that means the average error rate dropped from 9.9% to 6.3% across the 14 languages, and from 3.2% to 2.7% in English, according to Wispr’s internal benchmarks.

According to the company, teaching a model to recognize specific names and terms comes with a trade-off: the more it relies on that user-specific context, the more likely it is to insert those words even when they weren’t actually spoken.

Wispr notes that Canto-2 strikes a better balance between context and accuracy, improving its ability to recognize user-specific terms without substantially increasing the frequency of incorrect substitutions:

Canto-2 recovers hard names and terms accurately nearly 7 of 10 times, without more false insertions. It makes a third fewer mistakes across 14 languages, and has the lowest Hindi error rate of any multilingual model on Hugging Face’s open benchmark. It is 10 times the scale of Canto-1, and our biggest step yet toward dictation that’s ready to send without a single edit.

According to the company, the percentage of difficult names and terms correctly recognized went from 41% to 69% between Canto-1 and Canto-2, “without inserting them more often.” It added that this improvement holds up even as the user’s custom dictionary grows, with the new model correctly recognizing 92% of easier terms even with 1,000 saved entries.

Wispr also noted that it trained Canto-2 to handle real-world dictation conditions, including background noise, laptop and phone microphones, and sentences that restart halfway through, rather than relying solely on clean recordings of scripted speech.

When tested using Hugging Face’s public multilingual benchmark, Canto-2 achieved results that would have placed it third overall as of November 9. However, Wispr conducted the evaluation itself, and the model has not yet been officially added to the leaderboard as of today, November 25.

In its own internal benchmarks, the company says Canto-2 achieved the lowest average error rate among the competing models it tested across 14 languages.

Canto-2 is now available to Wispr Flow users on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android in the Americas, with the rollout to other regions underway.

#3147. Scott Aaronson says AI labs are sitting on cryptography ‘bombshells’

The computer scientist says he is sure the AI labs hold cryptography results, but not what they are. He also says he never confirmed a rumoured break of RSA encryption.

Computer scientist Scott Aaronson says he is “virtually certain” that leading AI labs are holding back results that would break some of today’s cryptography. He made the claim in a post on his blog, Shtetl-Optimized, on Wednesday. He also warned that he does not know what those results actually are.

“Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area,” Aaronson wrote.

Until he sees details or hears from someone at a lab, he feels “much, much less confident” about what exactly they are. TNW has not independently verified the claims.

The post followed a comment Aaronson left on his blog on Tuesday. In it, he said he had heard “many, many rumors” that one or both labs had a fast way to factor large numbers. That would break RSA, the encryption behind much of the web’s security. The comment spread widely on X, and he later added a note to it.

“A rumor is a rumor is a rumor, and the parts that I’m ‘virtually certain’ about fall well short of Factoring in P,” he wrote.

Google published a paper on Wednesday with a new factoring algorithm. Aaronson said it held big theoretical results, but nothing of practical use for breaking encryption.

The rumours come during a run of maths results from OpenAI and Anthropic. On Tuesday, both labs published proofs of VP ≠ VNP. The problem has long been seen as a step towards P ≠ NP, the most famous open question in computer science.

OpenAI also posted a paper claiming that the exponent of matrix multiplication is exactly 9/4. The 111-page paper says multiplying two n×n matrices takes at least n9/4/2 multiplication or division steps. The question dates back to Volker Strassen’s work in the late 1960s.

Last week, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he and Claude had proved the Riemann hypothesis. The Lean proof assistant has since certified the proof. In October, OpenAI said its model had disproved a famous hypothesis.

“I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far,” Aaronson wrote.

He asked readers not to let cryptography overshadow the maths. If their main worry was a Bitcoin wallet, he wrote, they should look for rumours elsewhere. He also urged people to accept that the AI proofs are real, now that labs back them with Lean certificates.

#3145. Apple pulls popular Chinese AI chatbot from the App Store amid child safety concerns

Following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In 2023, the Shanghai-based company released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active users across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles users’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

Ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, new downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after users exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the company’s plans to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

#3143. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday, and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new users and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

#3142. Canada adds C$700M to its AI compute fund, favouring home-grown clouds

The fund helps small firms pay for the computing behind AI and now favours providers owned and run in Canada.

Canada is adding C$700M to its AI Compute Access Fund, taking it to C$1B, with bigger subsidies for companies that use Canadian-owned computing. A first new call targets health and life sciences, and 45 more firms are getting C$52M from the fund’s first phase.

Canada is adding C$700M to a fund that helps smaller companies pay for the computing power behind AI, the government said on Thursday. That takes the AI Compute Access Fund to C$1B, up from C$300M.

The fund helps pay for the cloud computing firms need to build and run AI products. In its new phase, it pays more when they use computing that is owned and run in Canada. The aim is to create demand for local providers.

“Canadian ideas need Canadian computing power,” said Evan Solomon, Canada’s minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation.

The first new funding round is open to health and life sciences projects. Solomon also announced more than C$52M for 45 companies from the fund’s first phase, bringing its total to over C$118M for 89 firms. Last month, Ottawa also put C$2.5M into helping 25 Prairie firms adopt AI.

The money comes from Canada’s national AI strategy, unveiled in June. Ottawa has also pledged to bring 500 megawatts of its own AI computing online.

In October, it backed Cohere’s C$7bn funding round. Foreign firms are interested too: OpenAI has said Canada has the energy and land for data centres.

#3139. Check out this beautiful wallpaper to celebrate the opening of the latest Apple Store

Apple has quietly announced the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the company has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac …

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the company has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

As we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the company has averaged two new stores a year.

India has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow company-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

The plan worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each new store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

To download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.

#3138. Breakfast News: Talking Stocks Over Turkey

Our analysts on starter stocks, 2027 priorities, and the stock that gave them the ick.

By TMF Breakfast News – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:30AM EST

Money talk often finds its way to the Thanksgiving table. One cousin wants stock picks, an uncle is calling a crash, and someone who’s never invested wants to know where to start.

You don’t need a crystal ball to hold your own — just honest perspective from investors. So we asked our analysts how they’d build a portfolio from scratch, what drives their investing, and when a stock gave them the ick. Bring their answers to the table.

This one’s for the relative who just opened a brokerage account. Here’s how three analysts would start from scratch.

If I were starting from scratch as an investor now, I would build a three-stock portfolio that offers stability, diversification, and growth. Here’s what I would go for:

As one of the more value-oriented investors on the Hidden Gems team, I have quite a few stocks in my portfolio that could be considered to be excellent “beginner” stocks. But if I had to choose just three to start a portfolio with, they would likely be Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB +0.37%), Brookfield (BN +2.13%), and Realty Income (O +1.18%).

In reverse order, I would choose Realty Income because it’s an excellent compounder with a 30-year track record of excellent total returns, and Brookfield because it’s a great combination of reliable fee-based income and investments in some of the most promising types of real assets. Finally, Berkshire is like a well-diversified portfolio all in one stock, and I’ve said many times that if I could only own a single publicly traded company, it would be the one.

Each quarter, the Stock Advisor team builds our list of Foundational stocks: 10 stocks that can form the basis of a well-diversified Foolish portfolio. That exercise is essentially the same as deciding what to buy when starting from scratch. It should be no surprise then, that my answer is obvious: Amazon (AMZN -3.12%) and Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX +0.04%).

Both of these businesses bring scale, leadership, and a credible path to decades-long success. They balance sector exposure and business-model risk while still putting capital toward companies with clear competitive advantages that are representative of some of the best the stock market has to offer. Two stocks do not a portfolio make, but I believe this is a strong starting point for many investors.

We asked our analysts what’s driving their investing this year. Their answers are worth borrowing as you plan for 2027.

I will soon turn 54, and while I still feel like a kid, the fact is I’m not getting any younger. While I still love finding and investing in those great growth stories, I’m also slowly moving into more of a “protect your wealth” mindset.

Retirement isn’t even a word in my lexicon today; I love what I do and where I get to do it and will keep on doing it as long as the Fool will have me. But last year I set out to really focus on dividend exposure in my portfolio and 2027 is going to be another year where that remains a top priority. Rest assured I’ll be checking in on our Dividend Investor service quite frequently.

I recently read a book called Sport’s Perfect Storm: An Industry Now Totally Adrift, by Roger Mitchell.

This line caught my attention: “In everything, the past is always prologue.”

After several years dedicated almost exclusively to reading investment books, this year, I’ve concentrated my leisure reading primarily on business history, and simply history. Learning about the past will give me a better perspective when investing for the future. Plus, this new focus feels particularly timely given that this year marks the 250th anniversary of American independence.

As the late Charlie Munger once said: “There is no better teacher than history in determining the future. There are answers worth billions of dollars in a $30 history book.

I want to think through and take bigger, bolder investment decisions that will play out decades from now. I want to find the compounding decade busters! By doing the research and building the conviction, you can build the investment positions.

However, then it takes discipline and patience to see those investments play out over the next few decades. It’s often so counterintuitive: you get super excited about something new (the dopamine hit) and then you have to wait … and wait … and wait (the sugar crash). Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither was a truly Rule Breaking portfolio.

I turned 57 this year, which puts me within a decade of retirement. I also know that many workers are forced to retire sooner than expected. So it’s probably time for me to start reducing my risk by beginning to build a bond tent that will get me through the “retirement danger zone”: a time when a bear market could delay my plans or force me to sell investments when they’re down.

However, like many Motley Fool members, I much prefer investing in stocks, and see investing in cash and bonds as the equivalent of being forced to eat broccoli because it’s good for me. (I don’t like broccoli.) So I will spend this year finding the balance between being prudent and pushing the envelope.

Someone will ask if you’ve ever gotten one wrong. Here, three analysts share the moment a stock gave them pause, and what they did next.

Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) is one of my oldest, high-conviction portfolio positions. However, there was a period where I (along with many other investors) was concerned that its core search infrastructure might be unprepared for an AI universe disrupted by ChatGPT, despite it having invented much of the transformer architecture behind modern AI.

Today, Alphabet is positioning Google Cloud as a primary growth engine, with an impressive backlog largely driven by enterprise AI adoption, it’s designing its own AI silicon through its custom TPUs, and is successfully integrating AI tools that keep users within the Google ecosystem. While capex is substantial, it has the margins and cash position to maintain its trajectory without compromising a profitable growth story, and that’s a value proposition I continue to believe in.

I first researched Pinterest (PINS +6.54%) in 2019 and was instantly enamored with the potential. The user base was smaller than other platforms, yet growing fast. And it was undermonetized. I called it an “exponential growth opportunity” because it could stack user growth on top of monetization growth.

My investment thesis for Pinterest appears broken, which is why I finally sold last year. Plenty of smart Fools think I’m wrong, and that may ultimately prove to be the case. But its most recent quarter showed only 17% growth in ad impressions and a 4% drop in pricing. In my view, the platform is getting oversaturated with ads, and many advertisers still aren’t willing to pay a premium price after all these years.

I’ve long admired Oracle’s (ORCL -5.13%) specialized “RDMA” server technology that’s so well suited to handle AI workloads, and in the several quarters since I finally bought in, my shares have appreciated handsomely. It’s loaded with debt however, and I’ve looked to super extended debt maturities as a mitigating factor. However, a slate of 2025 and 2026 borrowings for data center build-outs bent my buy thesis — I felt the “ick” after some back-of-the-napkin math!

My thesis didn’t break, due to explicit capital allocation and free cash flow assurances the company shared at its 2026 Investor Day in late October. But I continue to train a critical eye on capital expenditures, free cash flow, and the balance sheet strength of the cloud-based tech titans I own.

None of the analysts claim to know where the market is headed next — and that’s the point. They focus on businesses, not stocks, and make investment decisions accordingly.

You can bring that exact discipline and mindset to Thanksgiving. If someone asks what the market will do in 2027, it’s fine to skip the guesswork. Shift the question instead and ask, which businesses they’d want to own for the next decade, and why.

That’s a conversation worth having over dessert. And for anyone just getting started, remind them that every great portfolio starts with a single first step.

From all of us at The Motley Fool, Happy Thanksgiving. Fool on!

If a younger relative asked you over pie for one rule or piece of advice to build real wealth over the next decade, what would you tell them?

Discuss with friends and family, or become a member to hear what your fellow Fools are saying!

The best soundbars from Sonos, Sony, Samsung, and more

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single TV in need of decent sound must be in want of one of the best soundbars. And, likely, you're here because you're sick of awful-sounding TV speakers — well, I've got the list for you. We've spent a lot of time testing the best soundbars to make sure you get the best bang for your buck.

The best is still the Sonos Arc Ultra. It's an absolute stunner of a soundbar, bringing great sound, lovely Dolby Atmos, and even slick styling so you won't mind it sitting under your TV. It does come with a big wallet-denting price, though — if you're looking to save some money, we'd go for the also excellent Sony HT-S100F.

But each soundbar we've listed here would make a great addition to your TV setup, so whether you're shopping on a budget, need something to work with your existing tech or just need a few more options to choose from, these are the best soundbars we've tested that I recommend right now.

The Tom's Guide testing team is an experienced bunch who love good sound. Here's why you can trust us to find the best soundbar for your needs:

From the time I built a surround system from the cheapest stuff I could find on eBay to reviewing the latest and greatest sound gear, I put a whole lot of time and effort into working out which soundbars are worth your money. I've constructed this guide with input from the rest of the team so that we can use our experience to guide you through your soundbar journey.

When I’m testing soundbars, I put them through their paces in our state-of-the-art testing suite, complete with a top-of-the-range Panasonic OLED TV and an array of 4K Ultra HD Blu-Rays. I’m looking for soundbars that make movies come to life — both budget-friendly and premium.

As a reviews writer, I put soundbars through rigorous testing by analyzing sound quality across various film and TV genres, connectivity options, and determine whether they're the best value for money. I love watching movies at the theater, so I like a soundbar that can closely replicate the sound via Dolby Atmos. I also play a lot of video games on my PS5 and there's nothing better than a soundbar that makes you feel like you're actually a sword-wielding samurai in feudal Japan.

Before we dive deep into the best soundbars, I just want to go through what we look for when we're testing them. We make sure to evaluate the soundbar in some key areas.

Setup: While it's something you're only going to do once, we want to make sure that it's as easy as possible to get working. Plug-and-play is the name of the game here, and if there are extra features we want to make sure that they're as easy as possible to use.

How big is it? Everyone's space is different. Maybe you've got a massive room with loads of stuff in it, or maybe your living room is more compact and minimal. You want a soundbar that's going to suit your space, and, more importantly, not going to take up too much of it. We check whether the soundbar fits under our 50-inch OLED Philips testing TV to make sure you're not going to have any size issues. Ultimately, it needs to fit on your TV stand.

Are there any extras? What's in the box, and are its contents any good? Some soundbars come with extras like surround speakers and subwoofers. I want to make sure that those extras are worth it, and that they're not just pictures to sell them at the store.

Sound: This is arguably the most important part of the soundbar, and there are a number of things we look out for here. How's the dialog? Is it clear, or muffled? What about the bass — are you going to have rumbling floors in your movies, or are there going to be problems with the low end? I love testing the sound portion because I get to watch movies instead of working; But it's still important when testing and working out whether a bar is for you.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is the best soundbar around. It's not cheap, but it's surround sound and Dolby Atmos performance beats just about anything else that lacks separate surround speakers. I'll almost certainly never watch movies with anything else for some time.

The Sonos Arc Ultra is more than just a soundbar. It's a fully fledged audio entertainment center that connects to your TV and just happens to be really good for movies and TV.

I particularly like how you can stream your music to it from any device — I frequently find myself spending a bunch of time listening to my favorite tunes from Qobuz and Tidal with it, thanks to its ease of use.

But it's really that epic movie experience you're looking for with something like the Sonos Arc Ultra, and you get it in spades. The Dolby Atmos with just the soundbar is unlike anything else around, and if you add in the optional surrounds, it's a game-changer.

I absolutely love watching just about anything with the Arc Ultra — although you will want to pick up a Sonos sub so that you can get the low-end grunt your movies deserve. It's not cheap — but it is so, so worth it.

SetupSetting up your Arc Ultra is going to take a bit more effort than some of the other options on the list. I found it fairly easy though, given the excellent instructions. If all you want to do is use the soundbar, you just plug it into power, plug the HDMI port into the back of the soundbar and the HDMI ARC port of your TV, and it should work without problems at all. I did have to change the settings in my Samsung TV sound menu to make sure that the device was set as the primary sound output, but then it worked with no problem.

If you want to use the excellent Sonos room correction settings, smart features, or to connect other Sonos speakers as surrounds, things will get more complicated. You'll need to use the Sonos App for these — and while it's not difficult, it is extra work. The room correction options also need you to move around the room while waving your phone around, so if mobility is something you struggle with, you may want to look elsewhere.

Once set up, you won't have any issues, but it's worth bearing in mind that it takes more work to get it working. It's all absolutely worth your time though, with massive boosts to sound quality and useful features within the Sonos App.

How big is itThe Sonos Arc Ultra is a big soundbar. It's very long, measuring around four feet long. I found it perfectly suited for TVs larger than 55 inches, although if your TV is smaller, things might look out of place.

There's less of a problem with the height. It's only about 3 inches tall, so it'll fit under most TVs without a problem.

Are there any extrasYou get the soundbar in a box — there's no included subwoofer here. Not that you really need one, though, given that Sonos has managed to pack some incredible bassy hardware into its slim frame.

If you want to enhance your movie-watching experience, though, you can add in a Sonos sub and surrounds in the form of Era 100 or Era 300 speakers. It adds to the cost, but it gets very close to dedicated home cinema sound.

SoundThis is the best bit of the Arc Ultra. I love the way that soundbar sounds for movies and TV, with some incredible body to the sound. I found the dialogue clear while watching the news and other TV shows, and it was excellent when listening to Sir David Attenborough talk to me about dinosaurs in Prehistoric Planet.

For movies, as you might expect, the Arc Ultra dominates. I discovered that even without extra surrounds, the Dolby Atmos was amazing, putting me in the center of a space battle in Star Wars Episode 3. The bass without a sub is surprisingly good as well, although if you really want to feel your movies you should buy the extra subwoofer.

It's pretty good for music as well, uncommon for a soundbar. There's plenty of space, thanks to the wider form factor, and the bar manages the low end of your tracks pretty well, too.

The Sony HT-S100F (HT-S150 in the U.K.) is a great-sounding soundbar for an epic price. It won't break the bank, but it'll increase the sound quality of your movies and TV far and above the sound from your TV speakers.

When you don't want to spend loads of money on a soundbar, something like the Sony HT-S100F is just what the doctor ordered. It's a lovely, cheap soundbar that does everything you need it to — make your TV sound better than the built-in audio.

It brings more clarity to dialogue, most importantly. Everything from your favorite movies all the way to news bulletins and everything in between become much easier to make out, perfect if you're struggling to hear what people are trying to say.

It's relatively compact as well, so you'll have no problems fitting it on your TV bench beneath most sizes of screen. Our tester found it super easy to use, with very few (if any) connection issues that sometimes plague cheaper devices.

It's not going to be as impressive as some of the more expensive options on the list, but it more than makes up for it with excellent clarity for all your watching.

SetupGetting the HT-S100F up and running is about as easy as they come. Just plug the power in, connect the HDMI port to the HDMI ARC on your TV, and it'll turn on automatically whenever you turn on your TV.

Erin did find that you might have to occasionally turn the bar on with the remote control, but it didn't happen enough to be a massive problem.

How big is itThe HT-S100F is designed for normal-sized televisions, and its compact frame will fit on most TV stands. It measures 35 inches long, so you'll be fine for TVs from 32 inches to 50.

It might seem a little small for larger TVs, though, with the screen dwarfing the soundbar beneath. You'll also find some minor sound issues with larger sets, as the picture feels wider than the sound that's coming out.

Height-wise you'll be fine with a range of different TVs as well. The bar measures just 2.5 inches tall, so it won't cover the bottom of your screen. If it covers the IR receiver of your TV, there's an IR repeater built in so that your controller still works.

Erin found it fit well underneath our 50-inch testing TV, although if you've got a larger TV set, you might want something slightly larger in the long run.

Are there any extras?In the box of the HT-S100F, you get the soundbar — and nothing else. You can't buy an extra subwoofer or surround either, leaving you with no upgrades for the future.

This makes it great for just a simple setup, and it keeps the cost down. There's a controller in the box as well, so you can connect Bluetooth devices and change sources without standing up.

SoundThe HT-100F isn't going to blow you away if you're a movie lover, but its solid, serviceable sound is a big step-up over your TV's built-in speakers. It makes dialog clearer, music sounds better, and sound effects are easier to hear.

For music, things weren't quite so impressive, but if you've got no other ways to listen to music in the living room, it will more than suffice. If you're looking for a cheap way to get much better sound out of your TV watching, then this is the way to go.

Sony's mid-range soundbar brings smarts and excellent sound to a more affordable price point. It connects to your Wi-Fi for wireless listening and includes a good subwoofer for some extra sonic grunt. It's excellent for dialogue too, with crystal-clear voice work for movies and TV shows alike.

Sony's line of soundbars can cost a lot of money — but it's the mid-range and cheap offerings that we recommend the most. This, the Theater Bar 7, is the mid-range bar, and it offers some great value for money.

For one, the 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos sound is very good. The included sub offers some extra low-end for those all-important explosions in action movies, and the surround sound is immersive and well produced. The dialogue department is where the soundbar really shines. Speech is clear and easily discernible over whatever else is going on on-screen.

There are also some useful smart features built in. You can connect to your Wi-Fi to stream music to the bar, and adjust settings from the app on your phone. As long as you don't expect the best musical sound, of course — as with so many soundbars, this is not a musical powerhouse but a rectangular movie hero. And that's OK.

Those with bigger TVs might also struggle slightly with the size. It's quite a compact soundbar, and that can affect the perception of sound in space when the image above it is much larger. Thankfully, the solid surround sound does a good job of keeping the effect to a minimum.

It should be noted that the Theater Bar 7 is not a cheap soundbar, but it's a great way of getting immersive sound without spending thousands on one of the range-topping devices.

SetupFor any normal movie or TV watching, setting up the bar is very easy. Plug it into the power, and then into the HDMI ARC port on your TV. Plug in the subwoofer and everything connects together with no hassle at all.

Nor is connecting the bar to the internet. Download the app, and then follow the on-screen instructions to get everything working properly. We recommend you dip into the settings menu from there and turn the bass up, and raise the surround height to 10. That gave us the best sound, although your room might require some fine tweaking.

How big is itThis is a fairly compact soundbar, measuring 37.5 inches long. That means that it's going to be dwarfed by larger TVs, but those measuring around 55 inches or smaller are going to be fine. Our testing TV is 55 inches, for example, and everything was fine.

The subwoofer is thin and compact too, so you don't need as much space as you might for some of the competition. It fits perfectly beside a TV unit without sticking out like a sore thumb.

Are there any extrasThere's one very big extra in the box beside the remote control — that lovely big subwoofer for the low stuff. There aren't any extra surround speakers though, because they're all built into the bar itself.

Features-wise, though, you've got the mobile app to go with Bluetooth and wired audio connections. You can stream music to the bar from around the house, should you want some music when you're not watching movies. You can also use the app to change key settings of the bar, like sound profiles and bass levels.

SoundSony's audio chops are well documented, and the Theater Bar 7 just continues the legacy. There's some lovely bass on offer here, with impact and depth whenever the action on screen gets thick and fast. We used the app to dial in the bass a bit, though; out of the box it was tuned a bit low. Your mileage may vary, of course.

The dialogue was what really impressed here, though. Speech was clear and bright no matter what was going on around it, be that a fighter plane screeching through the skies or a car chase in the Batmobile. That's not to say it's ever in your face. When the goings get calmer, the voices adjust to match. You'll never miss a word.

Not everything is rosy, as it generally isn't with most soundbars. Music playback is disappointing, with merely an "OK" in our review. It's not bad, but there's no drive to the music as you'll find with movies and TV shows. A shame, but not unexpected.

If you want a true surround sound package in one unit, then the 1300XMK2 could be just what you've been looking for. Its extra speakers attach to the bar itself, and then you can move them into position when you want to watch a movie. It's not cheap, but it's a movie monster.

There’s not really such a thing as a “bargain” when it comes to home surround sound. Instead, there’s value — and the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 brings the value unlike just about anything. Flexibility, a more affordable price than the key competition, and, of course, great sound.

The two ends of the soundbar can be disconnected and placed around the room, powered by their own internal batteries. If you don’t have the space for a traditional setup, this is a great way to enjoy immersive Dolby Atmos sound without a more permanent (and expensive) solution.

The soundbar itself is quite large, however. It’s very deep and rather long with its surrounds attached, so you’ll need a long TV stand and big TV to make sure it doesn’t look out of place. There’s a subwoofer in the box that you’ll need to find space for as well.

The sound is great. It’s immersive, directional, deep and clear. We loved it when watching a wide range of movies, from action to romance. There’s little this soundbar can’t do.

SetupFirst off, hit the gym before you place this soundbar anywhere. This is a 26-pound behemoth, so you might even want two people to lift it into place on your TV stand. There are some extra setup quirks as well, but they’re easily mitigated thanks to the good instructions and user-friendly design.

Once you’ve plugged the soundbar and subwoofer into the wall, you’ll hook the soundbar into the eARC port of your TV. The soundbar and sub should find each other automatically, but if not, use the connection button on the sub.

If you want to use the surrounds, pull them off the soundbar and place them around your room. Sound adjustment is done automatically. If you have any wireless connection issues, re-attach them to the soundbar to reset everything.

Streaming and Wi-Fi are handled by JBL’s ONE app. It’s super easy; we had no problems at all getting everything connected and working.

How big is itThere’s no two ways around it — the 1300XMK2 is a very big soundbar. At 40 inches, the soundbar is wide, and that's without taking extra surrounds into account. It’s very deep too, so you’ll want to make sure that there’s enough space on your TV stand that way. If not, we’d recommend wall mounting the TV.

This is a bar suited to much larger TVs, 65-inch at a minimum. Otherwise you’ll risk the bar looking too big, and your TV small.

Thankfully, you won’t have to worry about how tall the bar is. It’s short enough that most TVs will amply clear the top, so you don’t have to worry about the soundbar blocking the view. Just bear in mind that you’ll also want space for the surround speakers behind your seating position — they’re not going to work if they’re in front of you.

Are there any extrasYou get everything you need in the box. There’s the bar itself, along with the surround speakers. Unlike other models, from the likes of Sonos, this is a big bonus and means you don’t have to buy any further devices for some lovely Dolby Atmos sound.

There’s also a subwoofer in the box, along with all the cables you’d ever need for just about any circumstance. There’s a controller in the box, although we found that the JBL ONE app was a perfectly serviceable way of controlling the sound — or your TV remote through the eARC port.

SoundWith 23 drivers powering 11.1.4 channels, you’d hope the 1300XMK2 sounded good. And, sure enough, the bar sounds excellent. Those extra surrounds make sure that the sound is immersive and massive, while the sub adds impressive depth and bass.

The planes flying in Top Gun: Maverick made the room shake, and the soundtrack was bombastic during testing. The whole movie placed our tester directly in the movie.

Object placement is good too, making sure that everything is kept in the right place.

The soundbar was pretty good for music too, making soundtracks sound great, although it struggled slightly more with stereo tracks — but it's still better than most soundbars.

Want everything in one box but don't want to spend every single dollar you have? The QS750F is a great option, with extra surround speakers and a subwoofer for less than $1000.

Soundbars are expensive — there’s no way around that. You want to achieve the best bang-for-buck sound, right? Enter the Samsung QS750F. For a relatively low MSRP of $899, the QS750F gives you a soundbar, two rears, and a subwoofer, which is considerably more generous than Sonos or JBL.

As a result, the QS750F blows the competition out of the park. For under $1k, you get cinematic sound, with enviable width and immense bass. The QS750F sounds so good that we forgot we were supposed to be reviewing it.

Although it’s just a 5.1.2 channel configuration — considerably fewer speakers than JBL’s monstrous 1300XMK2, which boasts 11.1.4 channels and costs almost double — you probably wouldn’t be able to notice the difference.

SetupAs with every other soundbar, setup is a relatively quick process. Once the soundbar, subwoofer, and rears are unpackaged, simply connect everything to power and plug the soundbar into your TV using HDMI eARC.

Unlike JBL’s collection of premium soundbars, the QS750F’s rears aren’t truly “wireless” — sure, they connect to the soundbar wirelessly, but the left speaker must be connected to power. This is only an issue if you’re short on power outlets, extension cables, or if you want a particularly cable-free setup. Even so, you’re not going to get a better multi-speaker setup for less, so we think this is a worthy sacrifice.

The subwoofer is wireless, so don’t worry about needing to connect that to the soundbar with a wire. It’ll automatically connect.

How big is itAs you might expect, the QS750F is a large soundbar. This is true of pretty much every high-power soundbar — they’re designed to be able to fill large rooms with both size and physical presence.

The soundbar is 46 inches long and ten inches deep, so you’ll need to ensure it fits on your TV stand/wall mount and that your TV is big enough. I’d recommend anything from 55 inches up.

The subwoofer is effectively a 10 x 10 x 10-inch cube. We’d recommend positioning the subwoofer around 12 inches from the walls on all sides. You’ll need to play around with spacing to figure out the optimal position. Some setups come with configuration modes in the relevant app, but Samsung locks its proprietary Space Fit Pro behind post-2021 AI-powered Samsung TVs.

Are there any extrasThe QS750F comes with everything you need for a Dolby Atmos all-in-one setup. You get the soundbar, subwoofer, and two rears.

You also get AirPlay, Google Cast, and smart home features in the SmartThings app, which we’d recommend downloading. You can easily adjust playback modes and listening styles — movie, music, gaming, voice enhancement — to find what pleases you.

SoundAlright, now onto the most important part of any soundbar: its audio output. Thankfully, you’ll be pleased to know that the QS750F sounds utterly fantastic.

As the QS750F is a large soundbar, it’s intended for use in a large room. The side-firing speakers in the soundbar itself and the powerful subwoofer work together to create a wide soundscape worthy of a movie theater. Although there’s not as much height as width, the soundbar’s Dolby Atmos performance is still admirable.

The dialogue performance is a clear standout, though: I was never left wondering what was being said thanks to voice enhancement mode. This feature isolated dialogue well, and ensured even the moodiest and broodiest speech was crystal clear.

Most audiophiles will be the first to admit that soundbars aren’t ideal for playing music — me included — but the QS750F didn’t balk at the challenge. Although I’d much rather listen to music via my bookshelf speakers or headphones, the QS750F played every song with rich, pulsing bass, and would be good enough for a quick listening session or party.

Sonos' compact soundbar brings excellent sound with a slightly higher price tag than the old model — but the app is still a bit tetchy. Still, this great-sounding bar is a great option for Sonos homes with living rooms too small for the Arc Ultra.

The Sonos Beam Ultra feels like a statement of intent. The app works better than ever, the sound is incredible, and the surround sound straight out of the bar itself is top-notch. There are still problems — music sounds bad, and a lack of HDMI passthrough is a shame.

But this is Sonos on top form. The design is great, bringing that Sonos minimalism to a smaller bar than the enormous Arc Ultra. It’s perhaps a little more plain than some of the brand's other devices, but it's a handsome thing that’ll blend in perfectly with any living room decor. The traditional black and white colorways are still the only options, unfortunately.

And then there’s the way it sounds. It increases the Dolby Atmos effect with height channels, making for a more immersive movie experience that lands you directly in the center of the action. Add in a few extra Sonos speakers for a full surround setup and you have the perfect movie-watching experience for a smaller space.

It is expensive, mind you. The Beam was never cheap, but this one ups the price ante to make it a less compelling buy than other bars around this size class. And while Sonos app is much better than it was in early 2025, I’ve had more problems with it than our tester, with dropouts and other problems.

Setup is super easy. You just plug the soundbar into a wall outlet, and then an HDMI cable into the eARC port on the back of your TV. That could be it, if you’re not interested in any of the extra Sonos features.

To finish setup you’ll need to use the Sonos app, which is now much improved. From there you can do sound tuning setup amongst other things, like connecting extra Sonos surround speakers or a subwoofer for extra bass. It’s simple and easy to do, and the app will take you through it step by step.

This is also where you’ll stream audio to the device or adjust any settings. There’s no remote that comes with the soundbar — everything goes through the Sonos app.

The Beam Ultra really stretches the “compact” soundbar thing. It measures around 30 inches wide, making it a larger soundbar than some of the smaller compact options. That makes it perfect for TVs around 55 inches and smaller, though Sonos says it works for TVs up to 65 inches.

For larger spaces and TVs you’ll want the larger Sonos Arc Ultra.

In the box, you’ll find the soundbar, a power cable, and the HDMI cable. That’s it. There’s no remote, no wall mount — just the soundbar.

You can buy extras. Sonos speakers, the Era 100, 300, Sub Mini and Sub 4 all work as surround options for the Beam Ultra. I’d recommend the Era 100 and Sub Mini for smaller rooms if you want to increase the surround capability of the bar.

Unfortunately, everything has to come from Sonos’ rather enclosed ecosystem. You cannot add a separate 3rd-party subwoofer, for example. Shame.

The Beam Ultra is the best Dolby Atmos soundbar for its size. There’s real height to the sound here, making for a far better immersive bubble than other similarly sized bars. There’s width too — it’s a great way to watch your favorite movies.

Unfortunately, stereo music sounds straight up bad. That’s a shame, given that Sonos nailed it with the Arc Ultra — if you want to listen to music, you’re better off grabbing a stereo pair of Era 100s. It’ll cost you less, too.

I've seen loads of soundbars pass over Tom's Guide's testing table, and while there are some excellent options out there, not all of them can fit onto one list.

That doesn't mean they're bad, by any stretch, and they might just be the best soundbar for you. Here are some of the soundbars that we liked testing but didn't quite make the cut for the main roundup.

For the same money as Sonos's Beam Ultra, the Marshall Heston 60 is another compelling compact option. It might not quite reach the same heady heights as the Beam Ultra for movie watching, but it absolutely obliterates the Sonos when it comes to listening to music. It's just a shame that there aren't any surround speaker options.

Samsung's biggest and most premium sound is very good, offering excellent Dolby Atmos out of the box thanks to its included subwoofer and surround speakers. If you're looking for an all-in-one package for a Samsung TV it's a great option, but we believe the JBL equivalent offers a more rounded surround experience. If you're looking for the best soundbar surround sound, then look for the more expensive Sonos setup.

This mid-range soundbar brings excellent sound, but it forgot to bring the premium price. You won't get any smart features, which is a shame, but when it sounds this good, you won't really care. The sub in the box is surprisingly strong for this price point, and the bar itself offers solid surround for the dollars you'll pay.

The KEF XIO is one of the best-sounding soundbars we've ever tested. It's also one of the best-looking and best-built. "So why isn't it on the list!?" Because it costs $2,500. While I let that sink in for a second, I'll also tell you that the app experience is hit or miss. Still, if you have the dollars lying around, there are far worse ways to spend thousands of smackeroos.

LG's Sound Suite Dolby Atmos FlexConnect (phew) technology is very cool, and in the right room it can sound very good. Unfortunately, its core sound simply isn't up to scratch when compared to the competition, and the Sound Suite FlexConnect speakers are sold separately for a hefty premium. A proof of concept that shows its worth waiting for the sequel — but it needs some more time in the oven.

The Polk Audio Signa S4 brings a great sound and surprisingly solid Dolby Atmos for a decent price. The included sub is plenty bassy, and there's good spaciousness to the sound. It's a large bar despite its lower price. The comprehensive remote control is comfortable and easy to use.

If you want something that looks super sleek and tidy, then the True X Bar is a great option. Its Dolby Atmos performance is admirable, and the price is right. We reviewed the 40A, but you can find the 50A for around the same price now. It's exactly the same, but comes with a subwoofer. But you can also buy the 40A and add a subwoofer later.

Read our full Yamaha True X Bar 40A review

One of the best bits of most modern soundbars is that they're all simple to use in some form or another — but if you want something that you just plug in and use, then you'll want to avoid any with smart features.

While those smart features can make them sound better, or work for different types of content, they add complexity. An app might make it possible to access room EQs and the like, it also makes it more complicated for the end user.

Although we used to recommend avoiding Wi-Fi connections and apps if you just want to plug in and play, almost all soundbars now have some smart features. So I'd recommend looking for models that don't solely rely on those if the physical connection is your main focus.

First up, if your primary use case is music, go for a pair of speakers with an HDMI port like the Fluance Ri71. They sound much better than soundbars for music. You'll thank me later.

Now, for the other questions. TV users will want something that increases dialoge clarity and makes it easier to hear what's going on in the news. You won't need a subwoofer or any kind of surround support. The Sony HT-S100F above is going to be perfect for you, given it's not too expensive and works great for TV.

Movie watchers should look out for subwoofers and surround speakers. You want more space for your Dolby Atmos mixes and the subwoofer will help with the low-end rumble you get with movies. The Sonos Arc Ultra and subwoofer is a good option for you, or the JBL Bar 1300XMK2 if you want something in one package.

If you have a small room or use a small TV, you don't want a massive soundbar; that much should be obvious. It wouldn't fit, for one, but it would also make your TV look much smaller. And who wants that.

However, you also don't want a soundbar that's too small for your TV. Otherwise, all of the sound will appear to come from the middle of the TV, rather than from it's sides like it should.

You'll want to get a decently sized soundbar if you've got something between 50-75 inches big. Larger than that and you should probably consider either the biggest soundbar you can lay your hands on, or a proper stereo setup built around one of the best home cinema receivers.

#3136. How Much Is Jensen Huang Worth to Nvidia? The Stock Market Just Gave a Clear Answer

Jensen Huang’s return sent Nvidia’s stock soaring.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:34AM EST

Jensen Huang's saga just took another unexpected turn. Nvidia's (NVDA -3.91%) board unanimously voted to reinstate him as CEO, less than a week after explicitly saying it wouldn't. The message the board is sending is clear. Despite Huang's extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and with one of his subordinates, he is extremely valuable to the company. Just how valuable? The market's reaction to Huang's reinstatement gives us a clue.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

It's no secret that Wall Street loves founder-led businesses, but why is that? There are several reasons. Let's discuss two of them. First, founders, who often own a substantial portion of the company, have a strong incentive to maximize shareholder value. Hired CEOs do too, to some extent. That's why equity-based compensation exists.

However, founders tend to have more skin in the game. They wouldn't just lose their job if their corporation failed, unlike many hired CEOs. They would lose a substantial portion of their wealth. Second, founders often have a much deeper knowledge of the business they created, its characteristics, risks, competitive advantages, etc. That may give them an edge in leading the business to greater heights. According to some research, founder-led companies generally outperform broader equities.

So, Wall Street's faith isn't blind -- it is backed by data. That brings us back to Huang. He helped found Nvidia in 1993 and made it one of the most valuable companies in the world, and the corporation at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Huang is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in corporate America. That counts for a lot

That's why the stock soared about 31%, gaining nearly $1 trillion in a single session, after it was announced that he was coming back. It was the largest single-day market-cap gain in history.

Huang's return reduces the uncertainty tied to Nvidia's CEO search. Before the announcement, the market didn't know whether it would take six weeks or six months, and it was hard to reliably assign probability estimates to each outcome. The market abhors uncertainty, so the news had a major calming effect for many investors. That doesn't mean that Nvidia is out of trouble.

The company still faces major investigations tied to Huang's scandals, and the man is scheduled to testify before Congress soon. Still, with Huang at the helm -- and even accounting for ongoing regulatory probes -- the stock looks attractive. The first sign of that is Nvidia's financial results. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, Nvidia crushed expectations.

The company's revenue soared 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, with data center revenue rising 110% compared to the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin remains exceptional for a company of this size at 74.9%, versus 73.5% in the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP earnings per share jumped 111% year over year to $2.68.

The company's AI tailwind is not slowing down much, if at all. It expects $130 billion in revenue for its fiscal year 2027 fourth quarter at the midpoint, representing a year-over-year increase of about 91%. Sure, that's a lower year-over-year revenue growth rate than in its recent third quarter, and so is Nvidia's 2028 fiscal year guidance of 75% year-over-year revenue growth.

But investors should remember two things. First, Nvidia tends to post stronger-than-expected results. It has done so more often than not for the better part of three years. So, a predicted 91% year-over-year growth rate may turn into something above 100% -- in fact, the company's Q3 2027 guidance implied its revenue would increase by about 89.5% compared to the year-ago period.

Further, a decelerating growth rate may indicate tougher year-over-year comparisons rather than slowing demand for the company's products. Nvidia clearly still has a large market to tap into, and with Huang back at the helm, it is as well-positioned as ever to do so. And even after its 31% jump, the stock is down about 36% from the all-time high reached a little over a month ago. At current levels, Nvidia stock remains a buy.
