#3134. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

When you're pumping weights or running a marathon, you're going to want something to keep your mind occupied — and there's little better than the best workout headphones. Listen to music, catch up with your favorite podcast, or devour some of an audiobook. Whatever you're doing you'll need some buds.

There are loads of options out there, but some are better than others. Our favorites are the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, with their great sound perfectly pairing with solid ANC and a comfortable fit.

We've tested plenty more of course, and we've tested as many as we can. So read on to find out which headphones you should be getting for your next sweat-proof listening session.

AI seems to be the latest fitness trend, popping up in smartwatches, workout apps, and headphones. I wouldn't recommend picking up a new pair of earbuds for these features. My experience is the AI functions aren't very useful, and will likely change a lot in the next few years. So, focus on finding a set that feel and sound good, allowing you to focus on your exercise without distraction.

For a long time, Beats headphones didn't make me think of exercise. But that was before Apple redesigned the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 in early 2025 into what are effectively AirPods for workouts, with active noise cancellation (ANC), an effective transparency mode, and proper support for iPhone and Android devices.

The winged design of the older Powerbeats Pro has been replaced with over-ear hooks, which are a lot more stable. I'd sometimes need to fiddle a bit to get them on, but once locked into place, they didn't budge. And because the hook keeps some of the weight out of your ear, they were comfortable to wear for hours at a time.

Though the downside of this design is that the case is pretty big, and much larger than you'd comfortably fit into leggings or a pocket; fine for throwing in a gym bag, less ideal for carrying about, unlike the minuscule Beats Solo Buds case. But this one tops the battery up to 45 hours, while the Solo Buds case is just for storage.

The Powerbeats Pro 2 come with Apple's H2 chip, just like the AirPods Pro 3, so expect similar speedy performance, although I didn't find the noise cancellation or transparency mode were quite up to the flagship buds' standard. Though I did jump with delight at the use of physical buttons on each bud.

These headphones powered me through weights workouts, meditation sessions and long outdoor walks with no issues. I put them in and they did exactly what I wanted; good audio with no fuss. I don't run, but my coworker Nick Harris-Fry does, and found the Powerbeats Pro 2 a good companion for runs too.

The company leaned heavily into the buds' heart rate monitor at launch. It's neat, but you'll probably never use it. There's a small optical sensor built into the buds which is used to track your heart rate during workouts, but if this is something you care about, you likely have a smartwatch or Garmin watch that can do this better.

If you’re looking for some top-notch earbuds for working out that won’t break the bank, then look no further than the CMF By Nothing Buds 2. With loads of gym-centric features at a price that’s less than a fifth of some of the more expensive options on the list, they’re a fantastic way to keep fit while listening to tunes. Or a podcast. Or like, white noise. Whatever floats your workout boat.

At this price point, you wouldn’t expect to find anything with noise canceling, let alone ANC that works this well. It did a great job of keeping a noisy office at bay, so the pounding techno in the gym will be no problem. Outdoor runners, rejoice, they also blocked out traffic sounds when our tester, Ashley, took them out for a walk.

You don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears destroying them either, thanks to IP55 water resistance. You won’t be able to wear them while swimming, but anything you might get up to around your block or at the gym is no problem at all. Music, come rain or shine.

You don’t even have to worry about them running out of juice mid-workout. The quoted battery life from CMF is 12 hours — we found that around 5 hours of use left us with 60% remaining. Add in the 55 hours in the case, and you’re home free for super lengthy sessions.

They’re a little cheap-looking and the environmental noise canceling in calls is… not great. But then you look at your bank balance, realize that choosing the cheaper earbuds has left you with spare cash for a better gym subscription, and suddenly everything seems to make sense again.

They go in your ears, stay there, and play music while you get on with your workout. Better yet, they’ve done it for less than just about anything else around. What more could you want?

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the follow-up to our former favorite running headphones, the OpenRun Pro. These bone conduction headphones sound great, despite the fact they use vibrations on your cheeks to transmit audio.

While out running with the OpenRun Pro 2 (or most Shokz headphones for that matter), we found that the fit was comfortable and secure, so you won't need to continually fiddle with them and can focus on your training.

The downside to the headband-style design is that you can't adjust the fit. However, there's a smaller edition (OpenRun Pro 2 Mini) that has a shorter band for improved fit. But we were impressed with the comfort during runs, bike rides, and yoga sessions.

You don't get a charging case, but we found that the battery would last around 12 hours between top-ups, which should see you through most workouts. That said, if you like to dial up the volume to max, expect closer to 10 hours of power.

I'm not a runner, but my multi-marathoner coworker Nick Harris-Fry summed up his feelings on the headphones, concluding: "They’re my preferred running headphones at the moment because of the excellent fit, open design and good sound. If you just want running headphones with an open design, it’s the OpenRun Pro 2."

They can survive sweaty workouts and light rain, but if you plan to train in the wet or want a more multi-functional set that'll cope with a dip in the pool, the OpenSwim Pro are a good alternative, and they have onboard MP3 storage.

The AirPods Pro 3 are Apple's newest flagship headphones, and stuffed with more features than ever. There's live translation, voice isolation on calls and head gestures to control your phone. All of that's great, but it's the fitness features that really stand out.

Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, the AirPods Pro 3 now have built-in heart rate sensors. Unlike the Beats set at launch, you can actually use the sensors with a load of different apps, including (importantly) Apple Fitness.

The new integration with Apple Fitness adds Workout Buddy, an AI-powered 'coach' which sends you motivational messages and performance stats, like an audio-only version of what you'd find on the Apple Watch Series 12.

I'm generally skeptical about features like this, but our resident marathon runner, Nick Harris-Fry, actually seemed impressed with the heart rate accuracy, which informs a lot of the performance metrics on Workout Buddy and Apple Fitness.

Then there's the fit. Despite being popular workout earbuds, I've always found that AirPods need quite a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But that's not the case with the redesigned tip here, which Fitness Editor Jane McGuire said performed brilliantly on runs.

Despite being one of the first mainstream brands to launch water-resistant phones, the AirPods Pro 2 were surprisingly vulnerable, with just an IPX4 rating, essentially for splashes. The Pro 3 upgrade to a much hardier IP57 for dust and water resistance, so you can finally use them in the elements.

Like the AirPods Pro 2 before, the Pro 3 are still disappointing on the battery front: eight hours per bud, up to 24 hours with the case (while you got 30 out of the case on the Pro 2). It's not terrible, but the sub-$50 CMF By Nothing Buds 2 reach 12 hours.

The main reason I don't rate these higher in the list of best workout headphones is mostly due to the design — these aren't made for sports and they're not as secure a fit as you'd need for all high-intensity workouts. But for general use with your iPhone, including yoga, HIIT sessions, and casual runs, they're a great choice.

As Google continues to develop the Pixel-branded ecosystem of devices to rival Apple's iPhone and AirPods, it's no surprise that the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are the best workout headphones for Android, even if they are targeted squarely at owners of the brand's range of Pixel phones.

The key upgrade from the first-generation Pixel Buds Pro is the addition of Google Gemini, the brand's generative AI model. As it's still fairly new, it doesn't replace the older virtual Google Assistant, although in theory it can. But in practice, we found that it doesn't always offer the most accurate answers.

Features like voice assistants and hands-free controls are useful, but not essential when you're working out. Instead, it's more important that they stay in place as you exercise. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have a new wing on each bud to help them lock into your ears.

This would be great, but it doesn't quite reach the inner-top part of your ear, so we still found a bit of adjustment was needed to keep them in position for optimal noise cancellation. Google also claims to have improved the ANC, but it's hard to really tell the difference between the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and the original.

However, it's still effective, blocking out most noises except for some higher frequency sounds like crying babies and emergency service sirens. The sound quality matches the Pixel Buds Pro, although you may want to tweak the EQ to your preferences, as the default setting is a bit heavy on the lower end.

One other thing they have in common with the AirPods Pro is that they're not necessarily the best workout headphones if you spend hours training every week, as the fit isn't quite optimized for high-impact exercise. But if you're after a versatile option to wear at the gym and at the office, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 are a great choice.

Bone conduction headphones are cool, but they’re bulky. Your common earbuds sound great, but they have a habit of making it difficult to hear your surroundings. Open earbuds, like the Beyerdynamic Amiron Zero, are a great middle ground that offer solid sound while allowing you to hear the rogue bus that’s bearing down on you as you do your morning run.

They’re surprisingly secure, their silicone “hinges” holding onto your outer ear with little discomfort and no wiggle. Ashley, our tester, had no problem wearing them for hours and hours on end, partly thanks to their lightweight design. Just remember that these are completely open, playing the sound at your ears rather than in. Everyone is going to hear your playlist. Everyone.

The battery life could be better. There are 20 hours total on tap here, which falls down compared to in-ear options. You’ll be reaching for the charging cable more often than not, unfortunately, although you won’t need to pop them in the charging case as often with 6 hours of realistic listening time. Our tests pretty much confirmed this number.

Sound-wise, these are a great alternative to in-ear buds. There’s less bass than we might like overall, but there’s little else we’d ask for. The mids sound good, and the treble is solid as well. Don’t expect game-changing audio, but for open buds these sound great.

Even better, you can change the EQ. That’s a big bonus for something like this, and it means you can change the sound to your heart's content so that they sound great no matter your sonic preference. Five bands of adjustment, baby.

They’re IP54 water- and dust-resistant too, so you don’t have to worry about your sweaty ears causing any problems down the line. These are a good pair of earbuds that open you up to safer, more aware exercise — we really like them.

The workout headphones in the guide above aren't the only ones we've tested. We regularly try out workout earbuds so that we can recommend the top options that are worth spending your hard-earned cash on.

However, there are several other good options if you're after a bit more choice. These are the earbuds we've tested that didn't quite make the cut.

I really, really like these headphones. They're almost the perfect version of Beats' workout headphones, but the fit (ahem) isn't always perfect, and when they're only $50 less than the much more stable Powerbeats Pro 2 with fewer features and worse battery life, you're better off with the Pro 2.

Read our full Beats Powerbeats Fit review

The OpenFit Air 2 are great open earbuds, featuring solid sound and a comfortable fit. What holds them back from a full mention on the list is the fiddli-ness of the ear hooks — the clip-on design is superior if you're looking for something both secure and easy to wear.

When Apple launched these in mid-2024, I loved them, even though they didn't have noise cancellation or a charging case. But now these are only marginally cheaper than the much better Powerbeats Fit, and about the same price as the more feature-packed CMF By Nothing Buds 2, it's hard to recommend them.

The JBL SoundGear Sense have an open-ear design, so they sit on top of your ears rather than in them. We found this was fine for quiet environments or working out at home, but as soon as there was a lot of background noise from wind or traffic, it'd easily drown out the audio. They're comfortable and durable, but best-suited to indoor exercise.

Before investing your money in a set of workout headphones, you want to be sure that they do what they claim and are comfortable enough to wear during your training. That's why we put each set to the test before including it in the guide.

I've been testing headphones for almost ten years and know the most important areas to check out before recommending any pair. You really don't want them to fall out and get lost or need to continually adjust them in your ears.

So, we wear the headphones across a range of training styles, including high-impact runs (which can cause a lot of vibration and movement), intense fast-paced workouts and weightlifting sessions to see how they fare.

If they easily stay in place, they glide through this test, but it's not a write-off if they do move — headphones that struggle with runs may still make great weights companions — so we move into other areas, like comfort and sound.

For longer sessions, including runs, yoga classes and extended gym sessions, we check that the headphones are actually comfortable in your ears and don't leave you with ear pain or pressure headaches, which can happen with some sets.

Likewise, you don't want them to run out of battery mid-session, so we check how the battery life stacks up to the manufacturer's specs. For earbuds, we see how long they last out of the case and confirm how long the case can boost that.

When it comes to sound quality, even the best workout headphones aren't going to be a match for the best audiophile headphones in terms of clarity and detail. But that doesn't mean you need to put up with poor or low-quality audio.

We use a consistent playlist of music to help compare the headphones to other sets we've tested, which includes a variety of motivational dance music, dynamic rock songs, and everything in between, including the best new workout music.

There are a lot of Bluetooth workout headphones out there, so it can be a challenge to decide between them all. However, there are a few considerations to keep in mind that'll help narrow your options down to the right ones for your needs.

Firstly, it's vital that they stay in place during your exercise sessions. Some have ear hooks to physically hold them down, but others rely on clever engineering, a range of ear tips, or a specific set of materials to stop them falling out.

You also want them to survive some degree of moisture. If you plan to get sweaty, then you'll need a set rated to at least IPX4 for water resistance. But for outdoor workouts with a chance of rain, it's best to aim for an IPX7 rating.

Importantly, they also need to last the length of your workout. If you're doing short, high-intensity sessions, then you may only need an hour of battery. But with the right case, you may only need to recharge them every couple of weeks.

If long runs are more your thing or you're training for a marathon, you'll need a long-lasting set, like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, which are specifically designed with long distance outdoor runners in mind and last up to 12 hours.

And, finally, how loud do you like your workouts? If you don't mind some background noise at the gym, then a set of passive noise-canceling headphones should do the job, but most of the best workout earbuds have active noise cancellation (ANC) instead.

Earbuds with ANC cancel out the sound before it even hits your ears, so they're ideal if you want to zone out to your favorite tracks and focus on your exercise. But you may also want to hear traffic when you're out and about, so choose a set with a transparency mode too, which cancels most, but not all, noise.

In mid-2025, I had to do something hard; say goodbye to the Jabra Elite 8 Active. These were my favorite workout earbuds, but Jabra decided to focus only on business audio and no longer makes consumer earbuds or headphones.

I'd been using Jabra's Elite Active headphones since 2019, and for more than half a decade they comfortably sat atop my list of the best workout headphones. But we move. Times have changed, and they're gone (but still supported, for now).

You'd struggle to find a new pair now as most retailers have run down their supplies, but if you're after new workout earbuds, and to my mind, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a worthy successor (even if they do add an ear hook).

If you've been hunting for new workout headphones, you may have noticed that each set has an IP rating for water resistance. This stands for Ingress Protection, and it's a measure of how well the buds can stand dirt and water.

There's a standard format to the rating — IPXY — where X refers to the level of dust protection and Y relates to the device's water resistance. The dust protection runs from 0 to 6, while water ranges between 0 and 9.

Unless you're working out in very dusty environments, the dust protection is less relevant and most brands don't even test them against that part of the standard. Instead, you'll want to pay attention to the water rating.

Headphones with an IPX4 rating are protected against water, so will cope with sweaty workouts. However, if you want to run in the rain (or are worried about getting caught in a storm) then aim for a set with an IPX7 rating.

This means they can be submerged in water up to 1 meter deep for 30 minutes without damage. That doesn't mean you should take them swimming (you'll want some waterproof headphones for that) but dropping them in a puddle isn't going to do them any harm.

Our roundup only includes workout earbuds, but it's not uncommon to see some people train with over-ear headphones instead, especially at the gym. So, which should you wear for exercise?

Ultimately, it comes down to preference, but there are a few factors to consider. Over-ears use an adjustable headband to keep them in place, so they're not likely to move about, especially if you're lifting weights.

Even just a few years ago, in-ear buds weren't really designed with exercise in mind, so they'd often fall out or need a lot of fiddling to keep them in place. But the best workout headphones we've included here all have ways to overcome that challenge.

Some, like the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2, have ear hooks to hold them securely, while others use a combination of weight balance and grippy materials to prevent them falling from your ear mid-workout.

But many people also feel like a larger set of headphones will have longer battery life and sound better too. However, the performance gap has shrunk, so you can get impressive noise cancellation and battery life from workout earbuds now.

The downside to over-ears is that they're generally not designed for sweaty exercise. Many have leather ear pads, and these quickly wear with repeated movements and contact with sweat. You can replace them, but it's not ideal.

The earbuds are also lighter, so you're less likely to notice you have them in, while over-ear cans can start to press against your skull and contribute to tension headaches, unless they're specifically designed for comfort. Although that usually makes them less durable.

Generally, no. This is partly due to the intricate designs required to make small earbuds packed with batteries, sensors, and headphone components. But it's also because most brands don't prioritize repairability.

Many sets, like those in our best workout headphones roundup, are durable, so shouldn't get easily damaged. And since most offer some degree of water resistance, a bit of sweat or light rain shouldn't cause you any problems.

So any significant damage is going to come from accidents, like dropping a weight onto an errant bud. However, you may notice a drop in battery life in the longer term, which you usually can't do anything about.

The only way around this would be to pick up a set of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2, which may be the world's most repairable earbuds since you can replace seven parts, including the battery and outer shell.

All of the sets in our best workout headphones roundup are wireless and connect to your smartphone or other devices via Bluetooth. But you can still find wired sets, including the Apple EarPods, which look a bit like AirPods but with a cable and Lightning connector to plug into your iPhone.

Wired sets also tend to be cheaper, so you may be considering a set that you wouldn't need to worry as much about damaging or replacing. However, it's important to consider how you like to train before picking up a wired set.

To keep them connected, you'll need to have your phone somewhere on your body, either in a pocket, waistband or running phone holder. Consequently, there are two different devices moving at different times as you exercise; your earphones and your smartphone.

The movements are translated between them with the cable, so if you stretch your leg out, the cable tenses and may tug on your earphones, which could lead to them falling out.

Plus, if you're working out with weights or other equipment, there's also the risk that the wire will get tangled up, leading to the headphones falling out or the cable getting ripped.

Similarly, if you prefer to keep aware of your surroundings, you can use most wireless workout headphones in mono mode, with just a single earbud in while the other stays in the case. You don't have the same option for wired workout headphones.

Many runners would advise picking up a set of the best bone conduction headphones for running. Like the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 in our roundup, these use vibrating pads on your cheekbones to reproduce audio, leaving your ears free to pick up the sounds around you, like traffic and other people.

This is very helpful while out running, especially if you want to run safely in the dark. Although music can be a great motivator, you don't want to miss important alerts like emergency vehicle sirens or bikes coming up behind you.

Plus, it means that you're more aware of everything else going on around you, including other runners and pedestrians. And if you plan to run races, using bone conduction headphones allows you to chat with other runners and listen to music.

You can get similar effects with most of the best workout headphones, as transparency modes use the earbuds' built-in mics to elevate environmental noise, but bone conduction headphones also wrap around your head, so stay in place more effectively during high-impact activities like running.

If you want to prevent your earbuds falling out of your ears or slipping out of place, the first thing to consider if the type of exercise you want to do. For running and other high-impact activities like jumping, the most secure type of workout headphones are those with ear hooks.

These sit above your ear to prevent them moving or falling out, and so can cope more effectively with vibrations. This is also why many runners opt for a set of the best bone conduction headphones, since these wrap around your head to similar effect.

If you want more minimalist earbuds, then before you start your workout, you can adjust the silicone ear tips. Most sets come with a small, medium, and large replacement pair of tips so you can find the ones that fit your ear size the most.

#3131. Microsoft’s new Licensed Weights lets businesses customize AI models with their own data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft is bridging the gap between proprietary and open-weight AI while targeting data-conscious businesses.

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

#3130. Coca-Cola Is the Most Boring Stock I Own. After 64 Years of Dividend Raises, I'll Never Sell.

It's a blue chip dividend stock that you don't have to second-guess.

By Stefon Walters – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:39AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

I consider myself adventurous, but I often prefer boring when it comes to the stocks I own. I have my fair share of growth stocks, for sure, but my staple "boring" stock is Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%).

Although Coca-Cola is up over 40% this year (as of Nov. 24), its main appeal has long been its dividend. It has increased its annual dividend for 64 consecutive years, making it one of the market's premier Dividend Kings ( companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend hikes). Considering that and its sustained success, it's a stock I'll never sell.

You can count on one hand the number of brands more well-known globally than Coca-Cola. Its products (especially its namesake soda) are available in virtually every part of the world, and its asset-light business model enables it to operate efficiently.

Usually, if a company wants distribution somewhere, it needs plants, warehouses, and delivery fleets in that market. In Coca-Cola's case, it relies on bottling and distribution partners to do so. Instead of owning factories and delivery fleets around the world, Coca-Cola sells concentrates and syrups to its partners and lets them do the heavy lifting.

Keeping its business asset-light lets Coca-Cola maintain high margins and an ultra-safe dividend. You don't get to 64 years of dividend increases without consistent, high-margin cash flows.

Not many companies fit the "recession-proof" narrative, but Coca-Cola is one of them. Even when the economy slows and money is tight, people still buy their favorite Coca-Cola brands. That's the beauty of its brand moat.

And despite being the undisputed leader in its space, Coca-Cola hasn't gotten complacent with its drink portfolio. It constantly refines its lineup to adjust to changing consumer preferences. Just six years ago, it had over 400 brands in its portfolio. Today, it has around half of that.

When you have an option for virtually every occasion, you keep customers in your ecosystem. It's how the company has sustained success for so long.

Coca-Cola is a premium business that's priced like one. At the time of this writing, it's trading at 28.9 times its earnings, which is higher than its average over the past few years and higher than the S&P 500's (^GSPC -0.25%)23.7 P/E ratio. The stock is still a buy, but after a 40% run-up this year, the upside may be more limited. Luckily, that doesn't affect its dividend.

Coca-Cola is always a good long-term investment, but with bear-market fears lingering, a short-term silver lining is that the stock typically outperforms the market during sell-offs. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but Coca-Cola has strong momentum at a time when the tech sector is dragging down the broader market.

Get the most out of your TV using one of the best streaming devices

The best streaming devices are a relatively cheap way to upgrade your TV's streaming capabilities. If you have a non-smart TV, these HDMI-attached dongles and boxes mean you can use it to stream from all your favorite apps. But they're also a good option if you have a great TV with older software.

For most people, the best streaming device is the Roku Streaming Stick Plus. It has an app store, easy access to all your services and won't break the bank. If you're after a more polished experience (especially if you own an iPhone), then the Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is your best bet, but it'll set you back a lot.

These two are not your only options, though. We've tested the best streaming devices available right now, including options from Amazon and Google, to help you upgrade your home viewing experience without breaking the bank, and saving you from needing to replace a perfectly good TV just to get new software.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Roku's streaming devices have topped this list for a long time, and the latest Roku Streaming Stick Plus is only going to cement the brand's place at the top of the tree. The Streaming Stick Plus has loads of features that make it the best option around right now, from fantastic 4K streaming to a simple, slick UI.

This compact wonder brings powerful streaming without taking up loads of room behind your TV. Roku's user interface is among the best around, making searching through your favorite streaming services a breeze. The Roku remote that comes with it isn't the fanciest, but it's well laid out and simple to use, and supports voice commands.

The most important part, of course, is how good it makes your TV shows look. And, despite its lower price, we're happy to report that the 4K output is excellent. We combined it with a Samsung OLED TV, and it looked about as spectacular as you might expect.

Roku has slipped in some funky extras as well. We really like the screensavers — called Backdrops — that play when you're not using the TV. It avoids image retention and burn-in, which is a bonus, but it also makes what could be a big, black rectangle in your room something that actually adds to the decor.

The biggest drawback is the pesky ads. Make sure you turn off video autoplay, lest you be bombarded by irritating, noisy videos on startup. The ads are otherwise relatively easy to ignore. Despite the annoying ads, the Roku Streaming Stick Plus is an excellent streamer.

It's forty bucks. That's the pitch. It's just about the cheapest way to make your aging TV into a streaming powerhouse. There are fewer bells and whistles, and it doesn't have the highest resolution, but it doesn't cost much and means you can watch Amazon Prime, Netflix and more on your TV.

There are more features than you'd expect, though. While you won't get 4K, you do get some more premium sound formats like Dolby Atmos, should you be hooked up to a surround sound system. There are HDR formats galore as well, so the 1080p image will be super clear and colorful.

It's easy to set up and works speedily with the included remote control. It's not fancy, but it's cheap. And if you want to get the cheapest and easiest way to get streaming, there's not much better. Just don't bother if your TV is a smart TV — the built-in streaming is better.

The Google TV Streamer is a huge improvement over the old Google Chromecast. Similar functionality and navigation remain — and now you get live TV integration, tons of free content, plus several live TV services to choose from (YouTube TV, Sling and Philo).

But now, it also packs 4K UHD streaming with support for HDR and Dolby Vision for excellent picture quality, and Dolby Atmos for immersive sound. And with Google TV, you have support for over 6,500 Android TV apps.

That's not all, as the TV Streamer has a slew of smart home integrations that make it stand out. Directly from your TV, you can now monitor and control all your smart home devices.

We were able to view live streams from our various home security cameras and video doorbells, and also see which lights were still on — and dim them, too. You can even check the temperature on your smart thermostat. It's a step up from what other streaming devices offer and will make smart home enthusiasts gush the world over.

As with most newer TV models, Google has also incorporated its Gemini AI into the TV Streamer. This will do a variety of tasks, like providing simple summaries of whatever content is on-screen and pulling in reviews from both critics and the general public — for better or worse.

You can also use Gemini to create screensavers. Think of (almost) anything and speak it into the remote, and Gemini will create it for you, to amusing (or horrifying) effect.

One of the most surprising things about the 2026 Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) is not that it now comes with AI, but that it is twice the price of the 2022 version. That's an incredible jump in cost, even considering the price hikes we've seen across all areas of our lives. Whether it's justified depends on how much you use Apple's services.

Taking price out for a moment, the experience of using the Apple TV 4K is fantastic. It's uncluttered and easily links up to your non-Apple streaming apps like Netflix. Of course, one of the main attractions is how seamlessly it integrates with Apple's services and hardware, which is why it's the best streaming device for iPhone owners too.

Which brings us back to the price. Unless you have an iPhone or heavily use the Apple TV streaming service, it's probably not worth the investment. But the quality-of-life features you get with an iPhone make the price easier to swallow. Some of the smallest features on tvOS (Apple's software) are actually the best.

The included Siri remote uses an iPod-like touch scroller, which is great for navigation but pretty useless for text entry. So when you tap a text box, an Apple TV keyboard pops up on your iPhone, so you can easily enter usernames and passwords. But in theory, the biggest addition to the 2026 model is Siri's Apple Intelligence upgrade.

It's not hugely exciting, but it is a step up from Classic Siri. We tried Classic and AI Siri voice commands, asking for lists of movies with certain actors. Classic wouldn't get it right, but AI-powered Siri did just what we asked. It's good, not great, and depending on your views on AI, might not be worth twice the price of the 2022 edition.

We test streaming players by looking at both the content they can provide (most are very similar at this point) and how they deliver said content. Any streaming player worth its salt can load a 4K stream, but only a good one possesses straightforward navigation, robust search features and a wide variety of content to suit all tastes.

The first thing we evaluate is the setup, to see how quick and simple it is. From there, we take the user interface for a spin to see what content gets highlighted, what gets hidden, and how easy it is to navigate to our favorite channels.

As live TV service integration becomes a bigger feature in streaming devices, we look at how these sticks and boxes can place your favorites within closer reach.

We'll also watch a few different shows on a variety of channels to gauge the quality of the video and audio, to make sure they look good regardless of whether you have one of the best TVs or not.

After that, it's onto the extra features, like gaming, voice search and screen mirroring. These factors don't weigh quite as heavily toward the final score, but they're nice to have if they work well, and extremely distracting if they don't.

The main reason to get a streaming stick is that your TV is either missing a feature you want, or you'd rather not replace a perfectly good television just because it doesn't connect to the internet and download apps.

These are both great reasons to invest in these small and relatively inexpensive devices. After all, even the best TVs under $500 are still a strain on your bank balance, and if there's nothing wrong with your existing set, why send it out to the trash when you don't need to?

But if you buy a TV, you'll end up using the software that comes installed on it. With the best streaming devices, you have a lot more choice. Roku, Amazon, Google and Apple all have great options that you can use on any TV, and you don't have to be invested in each ecosystem to enjoy them (though it can help).

Generally speaking, the cheaper devices are supported by ads or feature-locked subscriptions/upgrades. But if you want to get what I'd argue is the best streaming device for iPhone owners (that's the Apple TV 4K), you'll need to spend more, but it's an entirely uncluttered, ad-free experience.

Although for other tech devices, there'd be a lot more between them, the choice here really comes down to price, brand and software. All the devices we've featured have apps for the major streaming platforms, so you won't miss out. Not that I really recommend AI, but the Google TV Streamer is ideal if you're a big Gemini user.

Or if you want to go the other way, I'd advise the Apple TV 4K — not because it doesn't have AI (the 2026 box has the new AI Siri experience), but because it's not that interesting, so you won't ever feel compelled to use it. I'm being a little unfair; it works with Apple's own services, but it's less reliable for third-party apps and services.

I've been using Ubuntu 27.04, and the speed boost is noticeable. Here's what else is coming.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful

With the repository added, you can install it with:

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

It’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

The best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

One of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which launched the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

It is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

It has a smaller footprint (wristprint?) than many other smartwatches, with a 1.3-inch display, compared to the 1.77- or 1.96-inch Apple Watch Series 12. It's not a huge amount on paper, but it makes a big difference, as it felt smaller and less noticeable on our wrist. It's a shame it doesn't come in a few more vibrant colors, though.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

The data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

Amazfit says that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking update.

The most significant change is that there's a new, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

These practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out new AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

Live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they said). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

Honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a new edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

That doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest update this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the new health and safety features that are the headline.

The Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's new "Health Guardian" suite.

Technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

What I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

The newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

It's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

If you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

Not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

Last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review

Apple didn't release a new budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful update from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

The Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review

We reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

We look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility issues with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

So we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the company says you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

Over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

In the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

It's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health issue does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a new smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

There are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

And that's one of the other big choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

#3125. Is Anthropic Joining the S&P 500? Here's What Investors Need to Know.

Don't expect major changes to your ETF portfolio.

By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:03AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share. The stock closed Nov. 20 at $88.91.

Given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent. It isn't, actually, and won't be for a while. But the stock will show up in several other major indexes within days.

When Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it. Typically, companies go public at much smaller market caps, not with market caps over $1 trillion. Index committees needed to decide whether to "fast track" these mega IPOs into the indexes sooner, given their outsize influence.

Several providers made changes. But Standard & Poor's did not. It elected to keep the existing 12-month waiting period and generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) income requirements -- companies need to be profitable in the most recent quarter as well as the sum of the past four quarters in order to qualify.

Anthropic, so far, falls far short on the GAAP income requirement, reporting a net loss of roughly $104 billion in the first nine months of this year.

Given these requirements, the earliest we're likely to see Anthropic in the S&P 500 is late 2027.

The S&P 500 will actually be the exception, not the rule, when it comes to adding Anthropic.

The Nasdaq-100 index updated its inclusion criteria as a result of the SpaceX IPO. Now, if a company's entire market capitalization ranks within the top 40 current constituents in the index, it can be added to the index after just 15 trading days. Since Anthropic is listed on the Nasdaq, it could show up in the Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ -0.65%) before the end of the year.

The Morningstar indexes, which acquired the widely-used CRSP indexes, could add Anthropic after the close of the fifth trading day. The Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.18%) would be one of the biggest funds impacted by this. FTSE Russell works on a similar timeline.

A lot of index funds will weight stocks according to the number of publicly available shares, not necessarily the total market cap. Since only about 5% of Anthropic's total market cap is now traded publicly, its starting weight will likely be small. Vanguard has projected only a 0.055% to 0.15% weighting for Anthropic in the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF.

When and if additional shares become publicly available, the anticipated weighting of these stocks would likely grow along with it.

If you really want to own Anthropic, you should probably just buy Anthropic.

The stock won't show up at all in the S&P 500 for the foreseeable future. For many of the major large-cap indexes and corresponding ETFs, the initial weight probably won't get much above 0.25%. The exception might be the Nasdaq-100, the Invesco QQQ ETF, and the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -0.66%). They could see an allocation closer to 1% given the more concentrated nature of that index.

It'll likely be a similar story to what we saw when SpaceX went public: a lot of hype but minimal impact to the ETF marketplace and your portfolio in general.

Long-term investors almost certainly shouldn't be making big asset allocation changes based on this. Even if you want to overweight tech based on a belief that Anthropic might spark the sector, your tech ETFs aren't going to meaningfully change in the future.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 777%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 199% for the S&P 500.

They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor.

#3124. SpaceX Sued by 2 States Over Grok’s Sexualized Images of Women and Children

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

People used Grok to generate millions of "spicy mode" images.

Oregon and Virginia on Monday filed lawsuits against SpaceX, alleging that Elon Musk’s company violated consumer protection laws, months after people used Grok Imagine to generate millions of sexualized images of women and children.

Grok Imagine is an image- and video-generation tool developed by SpaceXSI, a division of SpaceX. Shortly after launching last summer, the tool added a “spicy mode,” which enabled people to generate images and videos showing partial nudity and adult-themed videos. Grok Imagine is integrated into Grok, which is Musk’s AI chatbot.

In the lawsuits, separate but jointly filed, Virginia and Oregon allege that the sexualized images — including child sexual abuse material — were generated without the knowledge and consent of the women and children shown in the images and videos.

Read more: After Rampant AI-Powered Abuse, Grok Doubles Down

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in a press release that SpaceX misled people into thinking that their images and data would be safe.

“When xAI [now renamed SpaceXSI] allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

Donna Rice Hughes, CEO of child internet safety organization Enough Is Enough, praised Oregon and Virginia for taking action against SpaceX.

“It is abhorrent that women and children are preyed upon in this manner and even more repugnant that xAI’s Grok ‘spicy mode’ has not kept up with bad actors who abuse their terms of service,” Hughes told CNET, adding that Musk’s “team can find ways to prevent criminal misuse of Grok, and at the very least, disable Grok’s ‘spicy mode.'”

Grok Imagine launched on Aug. 5, 2025, and within months, it was used to generate millions of sexualized images, which were posted on the social media platform X, which is also owned by Musk’s SpaceX.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield alleged SpaceX “knowingly designed” Grok Imagine and promoted spicy mode’s lack of safeguards as a feature, not a bug.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material,” Rayfield said in a statement. “The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”

During a 9-day span starting in late December, Grok posted about 3 million sexualized images, according to an analysis from the Center for Countering Digital Hate.

In a statement posted Monday on X, SpaceX said that people using Grok to generate sexualized images and videos violated the platform’s terms of service and worked “aggressively to circumvent our safeguards.” The company said it tightened protections after the misuse and continues to test and adjust them as needed. SpaceX also said it notifies law enforcement authorities “when someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content.”

Earlier this year, several minor Jane Does filed a proposed class action lawsuit against xAI after people used their photos to generate child sexual abuse material using Grok via spicy mode. That case is still ongoing.

In July, a victim’s family also filed suit after photographer Russell Bloodworth in Arkansas allegedly used spicy mode to generate explicit photos of children. xAI went on the offensive, suing Bloodworth and South Carolina man Terry Wayne Harwood, who is also accused of using Grok to generate child sexual abuse material. The company seeks damages for expenses incurred in fighting lawsuits and for reputational harm.

SpaceX and xAI have faced lawsuits for other things aside from illicit image generation. The companies were sued for allegedly sharing sensitive data and for allegedly causing users to be hospitalized for psychosis after harmful chat conversations on Grok.

Monday’s lawsuits against SpaceX are among nearly 400 cases brought against 129 AI companies in the US, according to the AI Lawsuit Tracker. Many Big Tech companies have been sued for allegedly harming the mental health of adults and children. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a lawsuit brought by US states alleging the company intentionally designed Instagram and other platforms to be addictive to children.

Companies such as ByteDance — owner of TikTok — Snap, Google and others face more than 2,400 federal lawsuits alleging that their platforms harm the mental health of children.

#3123. Sketchy suggestion of ceramic iPhone 20 Pro

A sketchy rumor is doing the rounds suggesting that Apple is working on a ceramic edition of the iPhone 20 Pro.

There are no details, and while one concept image shows a ceramic back, this seems a rather unlikely possibility …

Fixed Focus Digital is one of those pointing to the possibility, stating that they have seen ceramic components for next year’s flagship iPhone. An image has also been shared by Tech Overwatch, which is very clearly a render, simply imagining what it might look like.

Details are very vague, so it’s possible that the whole thing is a misunderstanding based on Apple’s Ceramic Shield protection for the display and glass back, as seen on the iPhone Air.

Given that the iPhone 20 Pro will itself be a very premium device and involve a completely new production line setup, it seems rather unlikely Apple would want to either launch a super-premium version or experiment with two different versions at the same time. What are your own thoughts? Please share in the comments.
